en: Śrī. Now begins the second chapter.
(Therein, the first quarter.)

In the first chapter, the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) was explained because it is that upon which [the nature of] dharma depends; in the second chapter, the distinction (*bheda*) of dharma— which is dependent on those means of cognition— is stated.
By this, the sequential relationship between the first and second chapters has been established. // 1 //
(First Section: On the fact that the apūrva is conveyed by the verbal suffix; Sūtras 1–4) Sūtra 1:

Those words denoting action whose meaning is *bhāva*—from them the ritual act (*kriyā*) is to be understood, for it is this meaning that is enjoined. Sūtra 2: If it be argued that the meaning of all [words] is *bhāva*. Sūtra 3: [Response: No, because of the distinction between the two types of injunctions. Sūtra 4: Furthermore, because of the connection with the result. (Jaimini Sūtra 2.1.1–4)

Jaimini Sūtra 2.1.3: Those words whose application is found in their own form at the time of their origin are "nouns" (nāman); therefore, there is no further expectation regarding them, because they are already established in their own application. Jaimini Sūtra 2.1.4: But those words whose application is not found in their own meaning at the time of their origin are "verbs" (ākhyāta); therefore, [the action] should be understood from them, because the application depends upon them. *START MJaiNy 2,1.2-3*

In the first section of the first quarter of the second chapter, he formulates the first exposition: "In an injunctive sentence, the *apūrva* (the unseen potency) is conveyed by all the words [together]. Is it conveyed by each word individually, or is its conveyance by all [the words] as a single unit? (MJaiNy 2.1.2).

Because all [words] are connected with the result, and because they obtain connection with the principal [action], there is the cognition of a single [meaning] due to parsimony; however, the other words are subordinate to that. In this context, every injunctive sentence whose purpose is not directly perceived (adṛṣṭārtha) is an example.

In an injunctive sentence (*vidhivākya*), all the words that exist, without disregarding the relationship between action and its factors (*kriyākāraka-sambandha*), each individually convey the *apūrva*.
Why?
Because the *apūrva* is the result, and thus all the words are connected with that result.
If it is argued that even in the absence of the presentation of an *apūrva* (unprecedented potency), there is nonetheless a mutual syntactic connection between the action and its factors (*kāraka*),
we grant that this is true; nevertheless, what would be obtained is merely a connection with the primary element [the action].
Since the fruit is indeed the primary element— because it is that which is to be accomplished for the sake of the person (puruṣārtha)—

this being the position reached, we reply: because the apūrva is entirely unseen, when a scriptural passage can be explained by assuming only one [unseen factor], it would be a methodological fault (gaurava) to assume many.

Therefore, a single *apūrva* is conveyed by a single word, while other words are construed as being subordinate to it. Now, one might object: since the meaning of a particular word is what leads to the postulation of the *apūrva*, that word-meaning—by virtue of being the means to the fruit—must be accepted as being something to be acquired (*upādeya*), something to be enjoined (*vidheya*), and something subordinate (*guṇa*) with respect to the fruit.

If it is argued that, in the same way, for that very [word], since the status of being the subject (*pratyuddeśyatva*), the status of being the restated (*anuvādyatva*), and the status of being primary (*pradhānatva*) would also apply to the meaning of the other words which constitute the remainder (*śeṣabhūta*), there would result the fallacy of two sets of three contradictory properties (*viruddhatrikadvaya*); we say: not so.

In cases such as "One desiring cattle should sacrifice with the *udbhid*" (*udbhidā yajeta paśukāmaḥ*) or "One practicing sorcery should sacrifice with the *śyena*" (*śyenenābhicaranyajeta*), once it is understood that words like *udbhid* are names (*nāman*), they do not denote the means of the sacrifice; therefore, they do not bring about the set of three properties beginning with being the subject (*uddeśyatva*) in relation to the root *yajati*.
Therefore, only a single word is the conveyor of the *apūrva*.
Nor should it be asked why the *apūrva* is being considered when the discussion of the distinctions among *dharma*s has been set aside;
for the *apūrva* itself is what constitutes *dharma*.
He formulates the second position: "Does the cognition of the *apūrva* arise from words such as 'substance' (*dravya*) and so forth, or rather from a word denoting an action (*bhāvārtha*)?"
Since substances and so forth exist for the sake of the result, the cognition of the apūrva arises through that word.
Without the door of action, a substance is not connected with a result;
from the verbal suffix denoting the efficient force (bhāvanā), the apūrva is understood.
If it is argued that there is no *bhāvanā* apart from the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*), we say no;
for *bhāvanā* is indeed the meaning of the verb "to do" (*karoti*) as connected with the meanings of all verbal roots.
The meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) is the instrument (*karaṇa*) within that [action], as described by the words in the same syntactical unit.

The assistance rendered by substances and so forth is observed to consist in the production of the meaning of the verbal root. This is taught in such scriptural passages as: "One should sacrifice with Soma," "He gives gold to the Ātreya," "Therefore, gold should be worn," "One desiring to practice sorcery should sacrifice with the Śyena," and "One desiring cattle should sacrifice with the Citrā," and so forth.
In this context, the words *soma* and *hiraṇya* denote substances;
the word *suvarṇa* denotes a quality;
and the words *śyena* and *citrayā* denote ritual actions.
How can one understand the *apūrva* through these words such as "substance" (*dravya*) and so forth?
This is because substances and the like, being established entities, are capable of serving as means toward a result that is yet to be accomplished (*sādhya*).
However, the meaning of the verbal root (*bhāvārtha*), consisting of sacrifice, giving, and so on, cannot itself be a means, since it is itself something to be accomplished, just like the result.

Since substances and the like serve as instruments (*karaṇa*) with respect to the result, it follows that words denoting substances and so forth convey the *apūrva*. To this, we reply: substances are not capable of accomplishing a result without an action, for we do not observe firewood, a cooking pot, and other such items producing boiled rice in the absence of the act of cooking.
Therefore, the *apūrva* is understood through the verbal suffixes in expressions such as "he sacrifices" (*yajati*) and "he gives" (*dadāti*), which denote the productive activity (*bhāvanā*).
Now, is the meaning of the verbal root itself the *bhāvanā*, or is it something other than that?
It cannot be the meaning of the verbal root,
because that [meaning] is stated to be the instrument (*karaṇa*) with respect to the *bhāvanā*.
If it is argued that the second [alternative] is not tenable because an action distinct from the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) is difficult to discern,
do not say so.
Because it is possible to characterize the form of the verbal root (*karoti*) as being connected with the meaning of all roots;
as it has been said by the Teachers:
"Even though this [activity] is not perceived apart from the meaning of the root..."
"Nevertheless, it is understood only in its entirely general form.
Others have also said:
"The meaning of a verbal root is twofold for those two [roots], by way of both an accomplished and a goal-to-be-accomplished nature."
"cultivation (*bhāvanā*) has as its nature that which is conducive to the arising of something else, and it is of the form of that which is to be accomplished.
When "he cooks" is said, all people understand this meaning: "he performs cooking.
In that context, "cooking" [is the object].

The meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*), which is expressed by words such as *paktiḥ* (cooking) and *pacanam* (the act of cooking), possesses gender, case-role (*kāraka*), and number, and is of a perfected (*siddha*) nature.

That which is expressed by the word *karoti* (he does/makes) is devoid of gender and the like; the rule for the verbal suffix (*ākhyātapratyaya*) is prescribed in order to illuminate its nature as something to be accomplished (*sādhya*).
And that meaning of the verbal suffix is conducive to the production of the rice;
therefore, because it is the efficient operation (*prayojakavyāpāra*) of the rice which is the agent of becoming, it is expressed by the word *bhāvanā* derived from the causative form (*ṇijanta*).
Other positions regarding *bhāvanā* are untenable.
If it is argued that effort (*prayatna*) is what constitutes cultivation (*bhāvanā*), we say no;
for then it would follow that [the term] would be absent in the case of "the chariot goes.
If it is argued that vibration (*spanda*) is what constitutes it, we say no.

If it is argued that *bhāvanā* is a general property consisting in the cessation of indifference common to both [types of *bhāvanā*], this is not so; for there is no over-extension to the mental sacrifice (*mānasa-yajña*), which consists in the renunciation of mental objects.
Furthermore, there is no over-extension to verbal *bhāvanā* (*śabda-bhāvanā*), for an all-pervading and insentient word possesses neither motion nor effort.

The verbal productive energy (*śabdabhāvanā*) resides solely in the optative (*liṅ*), the subjunctive (*leṭ*), and the imperative (*loṭ*) suffixes; the objective productive energy (*arthabhāvanā*) resides in all finite verbs (*ākhyāta*).
As it has been said:
“They say that the optative suffixes (*liṅ*) and so forth denote a distinct *bhāvanā* called the ‘efficient-force’ (*abhidhā-bhāvanā*),
whereas another, the ‘objective-efficient-force’ (*arthātmabhāvanā*), is understood from all verbal endings.”

Furthermore, even those who maintain the doctrine of vibration (*spanda*) and so forth do not claim that vibration and the like are *bhāvanā* by their very nature; rather, they hold that it is a nature conducive to the production of something else. Therefore, *bhāvanā* is exactly as we have described it.

Just as in the case of "he cooks," [the activity] is conducive to the production of the result, which is rice, so too in the case of "he sacrifices," it is conducive to the production of results such as heaven.

And in that cultivation of the result, which is expressed by the suffix, the meaning of the verbal root (*prakṛtyartha*) is the instrument (*karaṇa*), because it is proximate due to being conveyed by the same word;
however, substances and so forth are not,
because they are remote due to being conveyed by other words.

Even the meaning of the verbal root (*prakṛtyartha*), though itself being something to be accomplished (*sādhya*), is capable of bringing about the result once it has been produced by its own means. However, for substances (*dravya*) and so forth, the assistance is indeed visible through the production of the meaning of the verbal root. When the result such as heaven arises through the instrumentality of the sacrifice and so on—which is denoted by the verbal root and brought into existence by substances and the like—that which consists of a favorable activity (*anukūlavyāpāra*) [is established].
This "activity" (kṛti), which is denoted by the word [bhāvanā] and consists in the production of a result, is not expressed by any one of the verbal roots such as *yaj* (to sacrifice) and so forth,
because it follows after the meanings of all verbal roots.
Therefore, it cannot be suspected that the root-meaning is the object of the productive activity (*bhāvanā*).
Let it be then— if you argue that the general meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) itself is *bhāvanā*— no, for its form differs with respect to each individual root-meaning;
for indeed, the favorability (*ānukūlya*) of cooking toward the rice is one thing.
Furthermore, motion [is the cause] with respect to conjunctions and disjunctions;

otherwise, the distribution of results would be untenable. While it may be granted that the universal "being an efficient force" (bhāvanātva) persists across distinct individual instances of efficient force (bhāvanā).
The general meaning of the root-base does not become that [efficient force] merely by this much.
Therefore, the efficient force (bhāvanā) denoted by the verbal suffix is indeed distinct from both the specific form and the general form expressed by the verbal roots such as *yaj* (to sacrifice).
This being the case, in the expression "one should sacrifice" (*yajeta*), the meaning of the verbal suffix is "one should bring about" (*bhāvayet*).
In that regard: "What should one cultivate? By what should one cultivate?
How should one cultivate?"

When this expectation arises— namely, "one should bring about heaven," or "one should bring it about by means of sacrifice," or "having accomplished the assistance through the kindling of the fires, the fore-sacrifices, the threshing, and so forth, one should bring it about"—

this entire collection of words recited within the context fulfills that expectation by providing the object (*bhāvya*), the instrument (*karaṇa*), and the procedure (*itikartavyatā*). Thus, the whole literary composition is merely an elaboration of the finite verb (*ākhyāta*) which expresses the efficient force (*bhāvanā*).
This very objective *bhāvanā*, possessing the three factors beginning with the object to be brought about (*bhāvya*), is called the "objective *bhāvanā*" (*arthī bhāvanā*).
All of this is the object to be brought about by the verbal *bhāvanā* (*śabdabhāvanā*); the injunctive suffixes such as the optative (*liṅ*) and so forth constitute its instrument (*karaṇa*).
The praise produced by the *arthavāda* constitutes the *itikartavyatā* (the manner of performance).
This very *śabdabhāvanā* is understood solely through the optative suffixes (*liṅ*) and so forth;
it has been stated that the *arthabhāvanā* is understood by all verbal suffixes (*ākhyātapratyaya*).
In that objective cultivation (*arthabhāvanā*), it is understood from the connection with the optative suffix (*kam*) that heaven is the object to be produced (*bhāvya*);
the status of the root-meaning as the instrument (*karaṇatva*) is understood through the direct statement of the instrumental case.

Thus it is heard in scripture: “One desiring heaven should sacrifice with the New and Full Moon sacrifices” (*darśapūrṇamāsābhyāṃ svargakāmo yajeta*), and “One desiring cattle should sacrifice with the Citrā sacrifice” (*citrayā yajeta paśukāmaḥ*).
And it will be explained that this status as an instrument is not possible without the postulation of an *apūrva* (unseen potency).
Therefore, the *apūrva* is understood from the word whose meaning is the "action" (*bhāva*), which ends in a verbal suffix.

The purpose of this inquiry, however, is that according to the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), there would be no substitute (*pratinidhi*) in the event of the loss or defect of the substance or other factors.
But in the established conclusion (siddhānta), however, there is the existence of that [the Veda]. // MJaiNyC_2,1.4-7 //
(Regarding the second section, on the existence of the apūrva, the sūtra: "But the injunction is the commencement [of action]. Jaimini 2.1.5.
The second section formulates [the inquiry]:

When there is doubt as to whether the *apūrva* exists or not, it does not exist, because there is a lack of proof; however, the fruit is accomplished from the sacrifice by virtue of the authority of the scripture.
To postulate that something momentary and already destroyed can be the cause of heaven is contradictory; therefore, it is better to postulate an *apūrva* (unseen force) as the means.
Whether it is called an intermediate operation (*avāntaravyāpṛti*) or a potency (*śakti*) produced by the sacrifice,
that which is termed *apūrva*— its distinctions should be understood from the ritual procedure (*prakriyā*).
In the preceding section, what was stated through the two interpretations (*varṇaka*)— namely:

"The word alone that conveys the *apūrva* is the verbal form ending in an optative suffix, namely the word ‘yajeta’ (‘one should sacrifice’), which expresses the meaning of the action. This is untenable,
because there is no evidence for the existence of the *apūrva*.

Since the instrument (*karaṇa*) and the productive activity (*bhāvanā*) are denoted by these two—the stem and the suffix in the word ‘yajeta’—if it is argued that, in the absence of an *apūrva*, it is impossible for a perishable sacrifice to be the means of attaining heaven which occurs at a later time, we reply: no;
for that is possible through the authority of the scripture (*śāstra*). This being the position reached—

We reply: By the direct scriptural statement (śruti) in the instrumental case, "by means of the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices," the fact that the sacrifice is the means for attaining heaven is established.
You must necessarily postulate a mechanism by which this is rendered possible.
In that regard, why should you postulate that the sacrifice persists until the fruit is attained?
Or is it that heaven is produced even from what has perished?
Not the first,
because the momentariness of the sacrifice is established by direct perception.
The second [alternative] is not tenable,
because one does not observe the birth of a son when both husband and wife are dead.
Therefore, our novel hypothesis, being free from contradiction, is superior to your hypothesis, which contradicts other means of valid cognition.

If it is argued that even if the *apūrva* (the unseen potency) is postulated, the scriptural statement that sacrifice is the means to heaven would be contradicted because that [potency] alone would be the means to heaven, we say: no.
This is because we accept that the *apūrva* is the intermediate operation (*avāntaravyāpāra*) of the sacrifice.
For the status of an axe as a means does not disappear simply because there exist intermediate operations such as the lifting up and the bringing down [of the axe].
If, upon the destruction of the sacrifice—which possesses an activity—the [activity] does not persist, then let there be some power (*śakti*) produced by the sacrifice, which is the *apūrva*.
Even with the intervention of this power, the status of the sacrifice as a means (*sādhana*) is not contradicted;
for it is accepted that fire retains its capacity to burn even when its heat is intervened by something else.
Just as the heat produced by charcoal persists in the water even when the charcoal has been extinguished,
so too may the *apūrva* produced by a sacrifice persist within the self of the agent even after the sacrifice has perished.
Therefore, the *apūrva* exists.
Its specific details, however, are to be understood through the sacrificial procedure established by tradition (*saṃpradāya*).

For instance, the procedure has been shown by the ancient teachers as follows: "First of all, the fact that the ritual action is a means to a result is indicated by the statement of the fruit: 'One should bring about heaven by means of sacrifice.
When the question arises, 'How can a result be produced by something perishable?', it is stated: 'By producing the *apūrva* (the unseen potency). "
In response to the inquiry, "How is the *apūrva* produced?", [the answer is] "by means of the mode of performing the sacrifice.
And that *apūrva* in the case of the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices is of several kinds: the fruit-*apūrva*, the collective (*samudāya*)-*apūrva*, and the six origin (*utpatti*)-*apūrvas*.
And regarding the *apūrva* of the constituent parts (*aṅga*):
that by which heaven is initiated is the *phalāpūrva* (the *apūrva* of the fruit).
On the new moon day (*amāvāsyā*), there is a single collective performance (*samudāya*) consisting of three sacrifices.
On the full-moon day, there is another [set of three sacrifices];

since it is impossible for those two sets, existing at different times, to jointly initiate a single fruit-apūrva (transcendental result), one must postulate two distinct apūrvas produced by the two groups for the sake of initiating that [result].

For the sake of initiating each of those two, since the three sacrifices belonging to each group exist at different moments and thus cannot form a composite whole, there are three separate origination-apūrvas (utpattyapūrva) produced by the three sacrifices of each set.
These [auxiliaries] must be postulated.

Since the sacrifice cannot be accomplished without the assistance of its constituent parts (*aṅga*), and since those parts—which exist over multiple moments—cannot form a simultaneous aggregate, the "unprecedented potencies of the parts" (*aṅgāpūrva*) must be postulated.

In this regard, the distinction is as follows: auxiliaries that assist by way of co-operation (*sahakārin*), such as threshing and so forth, produce excellence in the very nature of the sacrifice itself through the mediation of the preparation of the substance and the deity; thus, they bring about the accomplishment of the "unprecedented potency of production" (*utpattyapūrva*).
[The subsidiaries] operate toward the *apūrva* of the fruit by means of that [primary *apūrva*].
However, the remote auxiliaries (*ārādupakāraka*), such as the *prayāja* offerings, operate directly toward the production of the *apūrva* of the fruit from the *apūrvas* of origination.

Even though there is such a diversity of types, all the constituent parts (aṅgas) are auxiliaries for the accomplishment of the unprecedented result (apūrva); thus, they are accepted as having a single form through this mode of being (itthambhāva). In this very manner, the procedure regarding the unprecedented result is to be understood everywhere.
START MJaiNy 2,1.11-12 Here he states the opinion of the Guru: "The act of sacrifice, in its subtle form, resides within the nature of atoms."
If it is argued that the *apūrva* is not that which is called the "result" (*niyoga*), we say no to that.
The subtlety of action devoid of pride is expressed by the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and other such markers;
therefore, there exists an *apūrva* (unseen potency) as a distinct effect from the sacrifice itself.
[Response: That *apūrva*, which is designated as "niyoga" (an injunction), and which is intended by the Teacher, does not exist.
Why?
Because the fruit is produced even without that apūrva.
Nor should it be asked how the fruit is established if the sacrifice perishes.

The prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is as follows: "The sacrificial act (*yāgakriyā*) does not perish in its entirety; rather, existing in an imperceptible state as a subtle form, it abides either within the atoms constituting the substances related to the sacrifice—which serve to originate the body in heaven—or within the self of the sacrificer, and thereby brings about the fruit.
This is not tenable.
Because there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for the meaning of [the word] "utterance" (*ukti*).
Nor should it be suspected that there is likewise a lack of a means of valid cognition for the "injunction" (*niyoga*),
because Vedic optatives (*liṅ*) and other such suffixes denote that very injunction.
Therefore, one postulates an *apūrva* (unseen potency), which is distinct from the meaning of the verbal root and is the means for attaining a desired fruit that occurs at a later time.
(Third Section: The Distinction between Subordinate and Primary Status of Ritual Actions; Sūtras 6–8) These [actions] are of two kinds, being either subordinate or primary. JaiSū 2.1.6:
Those by which a substance is not intended to be prepared are primary, because the substance is subordinate to them. JaiSū 2.1.7.

"But where a substance is intended to be acted upon, there a quality should be understood [as the primary element], because that substance is the principal factor. (Jaimini Sūtra 2.1.8). The third section formulates the following: [The Sūtra] states: "But where a substance is intended to be acted upon, there a quality should be understood [as the primary element], because that substance is the principal factor.
(Jaimini Sūtra 2.1.8). The third section formulates the following:—
Is there an *apūrva* (unseen potency) to be produced by threshing and so forth, or not?
It certainly exists, just as in the case of "he sacrifices" (*yajati*) and other such acts; otherwise, the scriptural injunction would be rendered purposeless.

But when the removal of the husk is already seen [in the world], there is no new transcendental result (*apūrva*) based on the substance; thus, there would be a difference from acts such as *yajati* (sacrificing), for the statement produces a restrictive *apūrva*. In the context of the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, it is heard in the scripture: "He threshes the rice-grains" (*vrīhīnavahanti*) and "He grinds the rice-particles" (*taṇḍulān pinaṣṭi*).
In that case, grinding with water and sun-exposure produces something not previously existing,
because it constitutes the meaning of a prescribed verbal root, just like the meanings of verbal roots such as "to sacrifice" (yajati).
Regarding the opposing view: one should understand that there is a subverting argument (*bādhaka-tarka*) consisting in the futility of injunctions.

Since the purposes of removing the husks and making flour are already established in the world, an injunction for threshing and grinding would be redundant if they were intended solely for those ends.
Therefore, it follows that the *apūrva* exists. This being the position reached:
We reply: when a visible result is possible, an unseen potency (*apūrva*) should not be postulated.
However, the example of the sacrifice (*yajati*) and so forth is dissimilar;
for in that case, since the action is primary and lacks dependence on a substance, it is logical that the action itself is the means to the unseen potency.

In this case, however, because the word "vrīhīn" (rice grains) is in the accusative case—the case-ending denoting the object of the action—it is understood that the rice grains possess primacy as being the most desired end (*īpsitatama*). Consequently, the act of threshing, being dependent upon the substance, would produce an excellence (*atiśaya*) in the substance itself, rather than generating the transcendental result (*apūrva*). Furthermore, this does not render the injunction purposeless.

Even though the removal of the husk is possible by means such as scratching with the fingernails, there is a restrictive rule (niyama) stating that "it must be performed by threshing alone. Since this restriction is enjoined for the sake of producing an unseen potency (*apūrva*), there is no *apūrva* produced by threshing and the like [independently]. Thus ends the discussion on Jaimini Sūtra 2.1.13–14.
On this point, the teacher's view is stated: "Having broken down the second [case-ending] like that of the flour, the action is connected to the injunction."
One should not think that [the connection] is direct, because what is observed here is established through logical reasoning.

If it is argued that—in the case of "he offers the groats" (*saktūñ juhoti*)—one must abandon the predominance of the substance and, setting aside the accusative case, transform it into an instrumental case as "he offers with the groats" (*saktubhir juhoti*) so that the action becomes predominant;

and likewise, in the case of "he threshes the rice" (*vrīhibhir avahanti*), the primary action must connect directly with the injunction without the intervention of a substance by means of such a transformation—[we reply: no.
Not so;
for there is a disparity.
In that case, "no consecration occurs in the groats by means of the oblation," because it is impossible to employ those things that have been reduced to ashes for any other purpose.

With this intention, the status of being a preparatory act (*saṃskārakarma*) was abandoned. However, in this case, the preparation consisting of the removal of the husks is appropriate, because those [grains] which are freed from husks can be employed in the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*).

(Section on the Subordinate Nature of Sweeping and Other Acts in the Fourth [Adhikaraṇa], Sūtras 9–12) "But it would be a mere ritual act (dharma), because it does not produce a result, like the Prayāja offerings. (Jaimini 2.1.9) "Or rather, because the scriptural statement is equal, it should have the same character as the others. (Jaimini 2.1.10)
If it is argued that this is an instruction regarding substances (*dravyopadeśa*), [we reply]:
No, because it is for the sake of that [ritual], as is seen in common worldly practice, and because that [substance] is a subordinate element (*śeṣabhūta*).
(Jaimini Sūtra 2.1.11–12)

The fourth section formulates the problem: In the case of the injunction "He wipes the ladles" (*saṃmārṣṭi srucaḥ*), is this a primary action (*pradhānakarma*) or a subsidiary action (*guṇakarma*), given that no visible result [of the wiping] is perceived, as is the case with threshing (*avaghāta*)?
Subordinacy (*guṇatva*) is indeed not possible here; rather, there is primacy (*prādhānya*), as in the case of the *prayāja* offerings.
Even by assuming an unseen result (*adṛṣṭa*), subordinacy would be established by the accusative case-ending.
In the context of the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*), the cleansing (*saṃmārjana*) of the *juhū* and other ladles with *darbha* grass is prescribed: "He cleanses the ladles."
In that context, sweeping is the primary action (pradhānakarma).
Why?
Because it lacks the characteristics of a subsidiary action (guṇakarma).

And because it possesses the characteristics of a primary action (*pradhānakarman*). For the author of the Sūtras, having proposed two groups of actions, set forth their definitions separately in the Sūtras: “These [actions] are of two kinds, being either subordinate (*guṇa*) or primary (*pradhāna*); and “Wherever a substance is intended to be prepared, there a subordinate element is perceived.”

Because that [action] has the substance as its primary object, it is said: "Those actions by which a substance is not intended to be produced are primary, because the substance is subordinate to them" (Pūrva Mīmāṃsā Sūtra 2.1.6–8).
Those actions by which it is desired to produce or refine a substance possess the status of a subordinate factor (guṇa).
Why?
Because that action has the substance as its primary element;
it is a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "that for which the substance is primary."

In such cases as “he fashions the sacrificial post” (*yūpaṃ takṣati*) and “he establishes the Āhavanīya fire,” the substance—the sacrificial post, the Āhavanīya fire, and so forth—is intended to be produced.
In cases such as “he threshes the rice-grains” (*vrīhīnavahanti*) and “he grinds the rice-grains” (*taṇḍulānpinaṣṭi*), the substance—the rice-grains and so forth—is intended to be refined.
Because the opposite of what was stated applies to the *prayāja* offerings and others, they are principal acts (*pradhānakarma*).

This being the case, just as threshing is observed to be a purificatory act (*saṃskāra*) that effects the removal of the husks from rice grains, we do not perceive any such excellence (*atiśaya*) produced in the *juhū* ladles and other implements by means of wiping them clean.

Therefore, since it lacks the status of a subordinate act (*guṇakarman*) like threshing, it follows—by analogy with the *prayāja* offerings—that it is a primary act (*pradhānakarman*). This being the position reached—
We reply: the accusative case in "srucam" is prescribed for the object (*karmakāraka*).
And the status of being an object occurs when there is the state of being that which is most desired by the agent (Pāṇini 1.4.49:
"The object is that which is most desired by the agent").
Because the designation "karma" (object) is prescribed [for them],
and because the *sruc* ladles possess the status of being most desired (*īpsitatama*) as the means for accomplishing the sacrifice (*kratu*),
the *sruc*s are therefore the primary elements.
That being the case, the act of sweeping will have a subordinate action (*guṇakarman*) status, just like threshing (*avaghāta*).
If no visible excellence (*atiśaya*) were produced in the ladle (*sruc*), then an unseen merit (*apūrva*) would have to be postulated.
(Section 5: On the Primacy of the Hymn and the Recitation;
Sūtras 13–29) "But the hymn (*stotra*) and the recitation (*śastra*) are purificatory acts (*saṃskāra*), because they name the deity, like the *yājyā* verse.
(Jaimini 2.1.13) "But by reason of the purpose, it [the recitation] should be displaced, because there is no injunction regarding the deities, and the purpose is subordinate. (Jaimini 2.1.14)
Or rather, it may be for the sake of a subordinate quality (guṇa), like the word *vaśā*;
[this is not so], because of its inherent connection with the direct Vedic revelation (*śruti*),
and also because of the difference in designation.
And the quality would be purposeless;
likewise in the case of the *yājyā* and *puroruc* verses;
because in the case of the barren cow (*vaśā*), there is a connection with the actual meaning.
"Or rather, it should apply where there is purposefulness [Jaimini 2.1.21];
but not to those [mantras] that are traditionally handed down [Jaimini 2.1.22];
for [purposefulness] is observed [in the former case] [Jaimini 2.1.23]."

Alternatively, because of their connection with the Vedic revelation (*śruti*), the two verbs *stauti* (he praises) and *śaṃsati* (he recites) within the context (*prakaraṇa*) should enjoin the production of an action;
and also because of the distinctness of the words (*śabdapṛthaktva*). Furthermore, that statement [of the opponent] would be purposeless. (Jaimini Sūtra 2.1.24–26)
And another meaning is understood; Jaimini 2.1.27. And the denotation is like that of the ritual action; Jaimini 2.1.28. And there is the accomplishment of the fruit; Jaimini 2.1.29.
In the fifth section of the second chapter of the Mīmāṃsā-sūtra (2.1.18–19), he formulates the following:
In passages such as "He recites the *prauga*," is there subsidiarity (*guṇatā*) or primacy (*pradhānatā*)?
By that [reasoning], the recollection of the deity is observed; thus, there is the quality of both the hymn (stotra) and the liturgical recitation (śastra).
If the roots *stu* and *śaṃs* have the meaning of "recollection" (*smṛti*), there would be a contradiction of the directly stated (*śrauta*) sense;
therefore, even by assuming an unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*), their primary status is held for the sake of the direct Vedic statement (*śruti*).

In the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, it is heard: "He recites the *prauga*," "He recites the *niṣkevalya*," "They praise with the *ājya* hymns," and "They praise with the *pṛṣṭha* hymns. The terms *prauga* and *niṣkevalya* are names of specific liturgical recitations (*śastra*).
The terms *ājya* and *pṛṣṭha* have already been explained.
A *śastra* is a hymn of praise accomplished by means of a mantra that is not set to melody;
a *stotra* is a hymn of praise accomplished by means of a mantra that is set to melody.
It is appropriate that these two, the *stotra* and the *śastra*, are subordinate acts (*guṇakarman*).
Why?
Because, like the removal of husks, they achieve a visible purpose.
When it is argued that the deity is consecrated by the recollection [of its qualities] while the mantras are being recited—we reply:
the meaning expressed by the verbal roots *stu* (to praise) and *śaṃs* (to recite) is the proclamation of the connection between the deity to be praised and the praising qualities.
If the mantra sentences are intended to express this connection of qualities, [then they serve as praise].
In that case, because the primary meaning of the verbal roots is obtained, the Vedic revelation (Śruti) will be upheld.

However, when mantra-sentences are intended to reveal the nature of the deity to be recollected by means of their secondary qualities (guṇa), then the primary meaning of the verbal roots would not be applicable.

For in the world, when it is said, "Devadatta is a knower of the four Vedas," praise is understood; this is because that sentence does not have as its primary purpose the connection of a quality [to an object]. But when there is a focus on the person Devadatta himself—as in, "Bring him who knows the four Vedas"—[the meaning is different].
In such cases as this, there is no perception of praise;

for that [statement], by way of its connection with the four Vedas, is intended merely to characterize the nature of Devadatta, and thus lacks the purpose of expressing a connection with his qualities.

Furthermore, because the purport of the injunction would terminate in such statements as "one should manifest the deity with clarified butter" or "one should manifest the deity with the *pṛṣṭha* chants," the primary meaning of the verbal roots would be sublated.

Therefore, in order not to contradict the scriptural statement regarding the constituent elements (*dhātu*), one must accept that the hymn (*stotra*) and the recitation (*śastra*) constitute primary acts (*pradhānakarman*).
If it is argued that no visible purpose is seen therein,
then let there be a transcendental result (*apūrva*).
(Section 6: On the Non-Injunctional Nature of Mantras; Sūtras 30–31) Sūtra 30: The injunction and the mantra have the same purpose, because they consist of the same words.
Sūtra 31: Or rather, by virtue of its functional capacity in performance, the mantra must be expressive of the denotation [of the ritual act].
In the sixth section (ṣaṣṭhādhikaraṇa), [the author] formulates [the discussion]:
"And with those [verses] by which one sacrifices to the gods"— this verbal form (*ākhyāta*) indeed occurs within a mantra.
Or rather, it is not an injunction, because it is equal to another; therefore, it is not an injunction.
Since the power [of injunction] regarding words and the like has ceased, there are therefore three kinds of verbal expression (*ākhyāta*):

denotation (*abhidhāna*), primary action (*pradhānakarman*), and secondary action (*guṇakarman*). This mantra is handed down: “With those [cows] by which one sacrifices to the gods and gives gifts, the lord of cattle prospers and dwells together with them for a long time.”
The meaning is this:

the sacrificer, the lord of cattle (*gopati*), by means of those cows with which he worships the gods and those cows which he gives to the Brahmins, remains for a long time in the next world together with them.
In that regard, just as a verbal form residing in a Brahmin text is the enjoiner of either the primary action or the subsidiary action, [so too is it here].
If it is argued that the same applies to what is contained within a mantra,
it is not so;
for the injunctive power [of the mantra] is exhausted by the word "yat" (that which) and other such elements.
For when the word *yat* is present, that sentence is understood to be a restatement (*anuvādaka*), and not an injunction (*vidhāyaka*).
By the phrase "the word *yat*, etc.," the optative mood (*uttamapuruṣa*), the vocative (*āmantraṇa*), and so forth are included.
"I cut the grass, the seat for the gods"—this is in the first person. "O Agnīdh, distribute the fires"—this is an address.
In the same way, for the Brahman priest as well, one should cite: "He whose two oblations have met with ruin," and so forth.

Therefore, there are not only two modes— namely, that a verb either prescribes the primary object or prescribes a subordinate quality— but there is also a third mode, which is "denotative power" (abhidhāyakatva).
Therefore, that which is expressed within a mantra does not possess injunctive force.

(Regarding the seventh section on the etymological definition of *mantra*, the sūtra states: "The designation *mantra* applies to those [texts] that enjoin [the performance of ritual acts]. Jaimini 2.1.32.
The seventh section formulates [the following]:
"O wise one, [reveal] the counsel to me"—is this the definition of a *mantra*?
No, for it either does not exist or it does; it cannot be the latter because it fails to exclude over-extension (*avyāpti*) and other such defects. (MJaiNy 2.1.22)
The definition of a mantra, as unanimously declared by those who perform sacrifices, is that which is free from defects;

they apply the term "mantra" to such texts as those that serve as reminders for ritual performance. Regarding this, it is recited in the context of the *Ādhāna* (the laying of the sacred fires): "O Ahi Budhniya, protect my mantra."
In that regard, there is no definition of a *mantra*,
because it is impossible to avoid both under-extension (*avyāpti*) and over-extension (*ativyāpti*).

If it is stated that "a *mantra* is that which expresses a prescribed meaning," there is under-extension because the *mantra* "One should sacrifice *kapiñjala* birds to Vasanta" is itself of the nature of an injunction (*vidhi*).
If it is argued that the definition "a mantra is that which is the cause of reflection" suffers from over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to the *Brāhmaṇas*,
and similarly that definitions such as "a mantra ends with the word *asi*" or "a mantra ends with the first person [optative]" suffer from mutual non-pervasion (*avyāpti*),
this is not so.
Because the designation by the ritualists (*yājñika-samākhyāna*) is a faultless definition,
and that designation leads to the understanding that those [texts] which remind one of the performance and so forth possess the nature of *mantras*.
For instance, "uru prathasva" and others are reminders of the performance.
Verses such as "I praise Agni, the domestic priest" (agnim īḷe purohitam) are in the form of praise;
those such as "For food, thee" (iṣe tvā) end with the word "tvā";
and those such as "O Agni, come for the feast" (agna ā yāhi vītaye) are accompanied by forms of address.
"O Agnīdh, spread the fires"—these and others are in the form of injunctions (*praiṣa*).
"Was it below? Was it above?"—these and others are in the form of inquiry (*vicāra*).
"O Mother, O Ambikā, O Ambālikā, no one honors me"—these and others are in the form of lamentation (*paridevana*).

"‘I ask you about the furthest limit of the earth’ and so forth are in the form of questions; ‘They call the altar the furthest limit of the earth’ and so forth are in the form of answers. In this manner, other examples should also be cited."

In such cases, which are absolutely heterogeneous, there is no other common property (*anugata-dharma*) besides the conventional designation (*samākhyāna*), of which one could say it constitutes a definition (*lakṣaṇa*). Furthermore, the utility of a definition has been demonstrated by the former teachers (*pūrvācārya*): [text follows]
“Even sages do not reach the end of individual objects; however, the wise reach the end of those things that have been established by means of their defining characteristics.
Therefore, for those who are proficient, the definition [of a mantra] is the designation: “This is a mantra.”
(Regarding the eighth section, concerning the etymological definition of the term *brāhmaṇa*, the sūtra states:
"The word *brāhmaṇa* applies to the remainder. Jaimini 2.1.33.
The eighth section formulates [the following]:
"Does this definition exist with respect to that which is not Brahman, or does it not?
It does not exist, because there is no established limit to how many portions of the Veda there are. (MJaiNy 2.1.24)

"Mantra and Brāhmaṇa"—these are two parts; therefore, that which is other than the Mantras is the Brāhmaṇa. This would be the definition of a Brāhmaṇa. Regarding the Cāturmāsya sacrifices, this is recited: "These five oblations have Brāhmaṇas [explaining them] alone."
In this regard, there is no defining characteristic (lakṣaṇa) of a Brāhmaṇa. Why?

Because, since the extent of the Vedic portions cannot be determined, it is impossible to eliminate the fallacies of under-extension (avyāpti) and over-extension (ativyāpti) regarding the characteristics found in the Brāhmaṇa sections as well as other sections.
The previously mentioned portion of the mantra is one;
furthermore, some other portions have been collected by the ancients for illustration:
"The cause, etymological derivation, censure, praise, doubt, and injunction."
“Another’s action,” “ancient tradition,” and “the assumption of a restriction”: for instance,
“For by this, my dear, food is prepared” is a reason (*hetu*).
"Curd-ness consists in its being curd"—this is an etymological derivation (*nirvacana*). "Beans are indeed indigestible"—this is a deprecation (*nindā*).
"Vāyu is indeed the swiftest deity"—this is a praise (*praśaṃsā*).
He hesitated, thinking, "Should I offer it? Or should I not offer it?"—this is the doubt.
"The Udumbara post is to be of the same height as the sacrificer"—this is the injunction.
"Prepare food for me alone"—this is a *parakṛti* (an instance of another's deed).
"In former times, the Brahmins were afraid"—this is a *purākalpa* (a report of past events). "As many horses as one might accept... [and so forth].
One should perform the offering of four potsherds to Varuṇa for that many [days]; such is the construction of a specific determination.
Other examples may be cited in the same way.
Furthermore, the definition [of a Brāhmaṇa] is not "one who is any one among those beginning with the Hetu."
This is because causes and so forth also exist within mantras.
For instance: "For they desire you, O Indu" is a *hetu* (reason);
"The great ones have surged upward; therefore it is called water (*udaka*)" is a *nirvacana* (etymological derivation).
"The thoughtless man gains food in vain"—this is censure.
"Agni is the head of heaven, the summit, the lord"—this is praise.
"Was it below? Was it above?"—this is doubt.
"One should sacrifice *kapiñjala* birds" is an injunction (*vidhi*).
"He gave a thousand and ten thousand" is a traditional report of another's action (*parakṛti*).
"By means of sacrifice, the gods sacrificed with sacrifice" is a past event (*purākalpa*).
If it is argued that "a Brāhmaṇa is that which abounds in the particle *iti*," we say no;
for this would over-extend to the mantra "‘Thus you gave,’ ‘thus you sacrificed,’ ‘thus you cooked’—a Brāhmaṇa should sing [this]" (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 7.5.9.1), which is to be sung by a Brāhmaṇa.
If it is argued that "a Brāhmaṇa is that which is composed in a sentence containing the phrase ‘it is said (*ityāha*)’," we say no.
[This definition is flawed] because of over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to these two mantras: "The king indeed says, 'May I partake of fortune,'" and "Or the Rākṣasa says, 'I am pure.

If it is argued that "a Brāhmaṇa is that which has the form of a narrative (*ākhyāyikā*"), [the answer is] no; because this would lead to over-extension to such things as the hymn (*sūkta*) containing the dialogue between Yama and Yamī.
Therefore, when it is argued that "there is no definition of the Brāhmaṇa," we reply:

since it is accepted that the Veda consists of only two parts, namely the Mantra and the Brāhmaṇa, and because the definition of the Mantra has already been stated, it follows that the remaining portion of the Veda is the Brāhmaṇa; this is its definition.

(Regarding the ninth section on the non-mantra nature of *ūha* and the like, the sūtra states: "In cases where [the words] are not recorded in the sacred tradition, they lack the status of mantras; for the distinction [between mantra and non-mantra] applies only to those that are recorded. (Jaimini 2.1.34)
The ninth section formulates the problem:
Do the *ūha*, *pravara*, and names possess the nature of mantras, or do they not?
They are mantras because they form a single syntactical unit with them, yet they are not so because they lack the defining characteristics of mantras.

In the case of the mantra "I offer what is pleasing to Agni" (*agnaye juṣṭaṃ nirvapāmi*) used for a *saurya* oblation of cooked rice, the modification (*ūha*) consists of substituting another word, as follows: "I offer what is pleasing to Sūrya" (*sūryāya juṣṭaṃ nirvapāmi*).

Regarding the mantra "This Brāhmaṇa has been initiated" (*adīkṣiṣṭāyaṃ brāhmaṇaḥ*), at the time of its performance, they recite the specific name of the Brāhmaṇa and his ancestral lineage (*pravara*) as a supplement, as follows: "So-and-so Devadatta, son of so-and-so, grandson of so-and-so..."
"Grandson of such-and-such, son of such-and-such, grandson of such-and-such, great-grandson of such-and-such," and "belonging to the Aṅgirasa, Bārhaspatya, and Bhāradvāja gotras.
These variations (*ūha*), *pravara* lists, and names possess the status of mantras.
Why?
If it is argued that this is because [the mantra] forms a single syntactical unit with the injunction,
do not say so.
Because these [formulas] lack the definition of a mantra as it is well-known among ritualists;
for students do not study the *ūha* (modifications) and so forth within the Mantra-Section (*mantrakāṇḍa*).
Therefore, they do not possess the nature of a mantra.
(Regarding the tenth section on the definition of the *ṛc*, the sūtra states:
"Among those [Vedic texts], it is an *ṛc* where there is a division into quarters (*pāda*) according to the sense. Jaimini Sūtra 2.1.35.
(Regarding the eleventh section on the definition of the *sāman*, the sūtra states:)
In the case of songs (*gīti*), the designation [is based on that]. (Jaimini Sūtra 2.1.36) [This is the sūtra in the twelfth section concerning the definition of *yajus*:
In what remains, the term *yajus* applies. (Jaimini Sūtra 2.1.37)
The tenth, eleventh, and twelfth sections (adhikaraṇas) of the second book of the Mīmāṃsā-sūtra are formulated as follows:
When it is doubted that there is no defining characteristic for the Ṛks, Sāmans, and Yajus because of their mutual confusion—
Let there be no confusion regarding the fact that a *pāda* (verse-quarter), a *gīti* (song), and a *praśliṣṭapāṭha* (continuous recitation) are distinct.
This is what is traditionally taught: "O Ahe Budhiṇya, protect my mantra, which the seers know as the threefold Veda:
the *ṛcas*, the *sāmans*..."
"The sacrificial formulas (yajūṃṣi).
Those who know the three Vedas are "trividaḥ";
those who study what belongs to the trividaḥ are "traividāḥ."
The construction is as follows: "Protect that portion of the mantra which they call threefold, in the form of the Ṛgveda and so forth.
In this regard, there exists no fixed definition for the three types of Ṛk, Sāman, and Yajus.
Why?
Because the resulting confusion is difficult to avoid.
For the definition must be stated as follows: "A mantra recited in the Ṛgveda and so forth is an Ṛc, and so on," based on its well-known usage among teachers.
And that [definition] is over-extended (*saṃkīrṇa*).
This mantra, "May Savitṛ purify you with a flawless strainer, with the rays of the Vasu Sūrya," is recited among the *yajus* recognized as such in the Yajurveda;
yet it does not possess the nature of a *yajus*.
That [is] in the Brāhmaṇa, because it is designated as a *ṛc* in the passage "with the Sāvitrī-ṛc";
and having made the declaration, "He sits singing this Sāman," a certain Sāman is chanted in the Yajurveda;
furthermore, three *yajus* formulas—"Akṣitam asi," "Acyutam asi," and "Prāṇasaṃśitam asi"—are recorded in the Sāmaveda.

If it is argued that, because the *ṛc* verses which serve as the substratum for the *sāman* being sung in that manner are recited in the *Sāmaveda*, there is therefore no defining characteristic [of the *ṛgveda*], we say: no;
for the feet (*pāda*) and other such features possess unambiguous defining characteristics.
"Verses (*ṛc*) are mantras composed in meter and endowed with both syllables and meaning;
*sāmans* are mantras in the form of song; and *yajus* are mantras recited in a continuous flow, being devoid of both meter and song. When this is stated, there is no overlap whatsoever.
(Thirteenth Section: On the Yajus-character of Nigadas;
Sūtras 38–45) Or rather, the *nigada* should be a fourth [type of mantra], because of its specific characteristics. (Jaimini 2.1.38) And because of its distinct designation. (Jaimini 2.1.39)
Or rather, they are *yajus* formulas because they possess that characteristic form;
[this is established] by direct statement (*vacana*), by a specific feature of the ritual act (*dharma-viśeṣa*), and by the sense of the context (*artha*).
The designation is based on its quality;
[if it is argued] "it applies to all," [the reply is] no,
because of the specific designation as *ṛc*.
The thirteenth section (adhikaraṇa) is formulated as follows:
"Prokṣaṇīr āsādaya" (Bring the sprinkling waters)— this *nigada* is outside the threefold [classification].
And because the Yajus is recited aloud, it constitutes a distinct category; thus, this [Veda] is the fourth.
Because they are intended for communicating with others, those [utterances] which are loud are indeed *yajus*;

since they are endowed with the defining characteristics of that [class], the threefold division of the Veda is well-established. The following *nigadas* (proclamations) are recited: "Place the *prokṣaṇī* waters," "Place the fuel and the sacrificial grass (*barhis*) nearby," "O Agnīdh, spread the fires," "Spread the sacrificial grass," "O Indra, come hither," "O Harivant, come hither," and so forth.
A *nigada* is a mantra intended for communicating with others;
these are of a fourth type, existing outside of the previously mentioned *ṛc*, *yajus*, and *sāman*.
Why is this so?
Because the characteristics of *ṛc* and *sāman*—namely, being sung to a meter (*pādagīti*)—are absent;

and although the characteristic of *yajus*, namely being recited in a continuous flow (*praśliṣṭapāṭha*), is present, its inclusion within the *yajus* category is untenable due to a difference in ritual property (*dharmabheda*).
For there is indeed a difference in ritual property between "in a low voice with the *yajus*" and "aloud with the *nigada*. This being the position reached—

We reply: Just as in the case of the statement, "Let the Brahmins be fed outside" and "But the wandering mendicants (parivrājakas) inside," although the wandering mendicants possess Brahminhood (*brāhmaṇya*), there is a distinction based on their specific honor; in the same way, since the *nigadas* possess the characteristics of the *yajus*, they are indeed *yajus* themselves, and the property of being recited loudly (*uccaiṣtva*) is for the purpose of communicating to others.
Therefore, the threefold nature of mantras is well-established.
(Section on the Definition of Unity of Sentence, Sūtra 14:
"A sentence is one because of the unity of its purpose, provided that it would remain expectant if divided. Jaimini 2.1.46.
He formulates the fourteenth topic:
Is the sentence "devasya tvā" distinct or is it one?
It is distinct here because the factor that establishes its unity is difficult to discern. (MJaiNy_2.1.30)
When there is a division [of sentences], the criterion for having a single meaning is that the parts are mutually expectant (*sākāṅkṣa*).
Therefore, by this [criterion], the unity of the sentence is established, and the end of the *yajus* formula is determined.
In the context of the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*), it is recited: [text follows]...
“In the impulse of the god Savitṛ,
with the arms of the Aśvins,
with the hands of Pūṣan.”
"I pour it out as something pleasing to Agni.
In this case, the sentences ought to be distinct.
Why?
Because that which determines oneness is difficult to understand.
If it is argued that unity of meaning is the determinant for unity of sentence, we say no; for this would result in over-extension to a single word.
If it is argued that, since a collection of words constitutes a sentence, there would be a split of the sentence (vākyabheda) here because many such collections are possible, we say:
not so.

"Since it is possible for the agent [who utters the words] to understand that 'that which is expectant when divided and forms a single meaning when undivided is a single sentence,' the definition would otherwise suffer from over-extension (*ativyāpti*) if one were to state merely that 'it is expectant when divided.'"
In the mantra: "I prepare a pleasant seat for you; with a stream of ghee I fashion it as a comfortable resting place.

Sit upon it, O immortal one; take your stand, being well-disposed, O essence of rice," when the group of words beginning with "upon it" (*tasmin*) is analyzed, the term "having a single meaning" (*ekārtham*) is stated in order to exclude [the application of] that [definition] for the purpose of determining the referent of the word *tat* (*tad*), which denotes the subject under discussion (*prakṛta*).
For there is no single purpose in those two;
the purpose of the former group is the preparation of the seat, while the purpose of the latter group is the placing of the sacrificial cake.
*Syonaṃ* means level and even. *Susevam* means well-suited for service.
*Medha* means the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*), which is the essence; this is the meaning.

In this context, two sentences consisting of two collections [of words] are established for both disputants; these are excluded by the phrase "having a single meaning" (*ekārtham*). If "having a single meaning" were stated alone, there would be over-extension (*ativyāpti*).

Since the referents of the two sets of words— "May Bhaga divide for you" and "May Pūṣan divide for you"— which are accepted as mantras for the act of division, consist in a single object, namely the division of the substance,
the phrase "expectant with respect to the division" was stated in order to distinguish that specific substance.

In the present case, however, when the collection beginning with "to Agni, the agreeable" (*agnaye juṣṭam*) is separated, the preceding collection beginning with "by the impulse of the god" (*devasya tvā*) becomes expectant [of completion]. But when they are unified, the entire group has only one purpose: the act of offering (*nirvāpa*).
By this determination of syntactic unity (*ekavākyatva*), it is possible to ascertain the conclusion of a *yajus* whose extent is otherwise indefinite.
(Sūtra in the fifteenth section concerning the division of sentences: "In the case of equal [independent] statements, there would be a division of sentences. (Jaimini 2.1.47)
The fifteenth section formulates the argument:

Is the mantra beginning with "iṣe tvā" one, or is it divided? It is one because, in the absence of a verb, it does not cause the recollection of an action, and thus only a single unseen merit (adṛṣṭa) needs to be postulated. (Mīmāṃsā-jaiminīya-nyāyamālā-vistara 2.1.32)
These two [mantras] are enjoined by the verbal injunctions for the acts of cutting and wiping;
because they serve as reminders of what has been brought to mind, there is no difference in the mantras due to a difference in their purposes.
(Mīmāṃsā Nyāya Prakāśa 2.1.33) The text "iṣe tvā ūrje tvā" is heard [in the Veda].
Thus, this collection of words constitutes a single mantra.
Why?
Because, since the transcendental result (*adṛṣṭa*) of this mantra is singular, it is simpler (*lāghava*) to postulate only one such result.

Furthermore, it is not possible for these [mantras] to serve as reminders of things to be performed, as is the case with mantras such as "uru prathasva," because, due to the absence of a verb of action, there is no cognition of such a purpose. This being the position reached, we reply: "With 'iṣe tvā' he cuts... [and so on].
With the words "For strength, thee," he strokes [the branch]; thus, these two [formulas] are enjoined for the cutting and the wiping of the *palāśa* branch.

Consequently, when the verbal form "I cut" (*chinadmi*) is supplied in accordance with them, there is a division of the *yajus* mantra due to the difference in meaning, because they serve as reminders of distinct objects to be performed.
The difference in meaning is as follows: "O *palāśa* branch, I cut you for the sake of desired food," and "I wipe you for the sake of *ūrj*—that is, for sap, nourishment, or strength."

Thus, in passages such as "May life be perfected by the sacrifice" (*āyuryajñena kalpatām*) and "May breath be perfected by the sacrifice" (*prāṇo yajñena kalpatām*), although the general meaning of "perfection" (*kḷpti*) is one and the same, there is a clear distinction between the objects— life, breath, and so forth— and consequently a distinction between the meanings and the sentences. Furthermore, because the plural number of "perfections" is enjoined in the injunction "He causes [the sacrificer] to recite the perfections" (*kḷptīrvācayati*), a division of the *yajus* formulas must be recognized.
(Regarding the sixteenth [or seventeenth] supplementary section, the sūtra states: "The *anuṣaṅga* (supplementation) completes the sentence, because it applies equally to all. (Jaimini 2.1.48)
In the sixteenth section, he formulates [the following]:
"Regarding *yā te agne rajaḥ*, is there an ellipsis (*adhyāhāraḥ*) or an ellipsis-filling connection (*anuṣañjanam*)?"
Because the word "tanūḥ" is supplementary to another, its supply here is based on common worldly usage.
The expectation of the Veda must be fulfilled by the Veda itself; this is the necessary connection (*anuṣañjana*).
Even that which is subordinate to something else, when situated within the Veda, possesses this quality, whereas that which is worldly does not.
In the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, regarding the *upasat* oblations, it is thus recorded in the scripture: [text continues]
“O Agni, that body of yours which dwells in the raw [unbaked] clay, most excellent, dwelling in the depths—
let it drive away the fierce word, let it drive away the terrible word, svāhā! O Agni, that body of yours which dwells in the dust...”
"O Agni, that form of yours which rests in iron..."—the meaning of this is as follows: "Agni has three bodies fashioned from iron, silver, and gold;
among these, the first body mentioned here is exceedingly vast."

"Abiding in that subtle form within the sharp, piercing metal, I have destroyed by that body both hunger and thirst— which are minor offenses— as well as the great sins such as the killing of a hero. And so says the Brāhmaṇa:
“That fierce word which he has struck away, that brilliant word which he has struck away—svāhā!
Hunger and thirst, indeed, are the fierce word;
sin and the slaying of a kinsman are the brilliant word.”
In that context, the first mantra, which ends with *svāhā*, is complete as a sentence; therefore, nothing further needs to be supplied.
Indeed, the portion beginning with "tanūr varṣiṣṭhā" is not fit to be construed with those two [mantras], because it is a supplement to the first mantra.
This being the position reached, we reply: the expectancy of two Vedic mantras must be fulfilled by a Vedic supplementary passage (vākyaśeṣa) alone.
Therefore, the portion beginning with "tanūrvarṣiṣṭhā" is to be supplied as an *anuṣaṅga* (supplementation) to the latter two mantras.

Even though this [word] belongs to another [sentence] as a remainder, nevertheless, being situated in the context of the Buddha [the preceding sentence], it is brought closer by way of mental supply (*adhyāhāra*) from what is to be supplied;
therefore, an *anuṣaṅga* (supplying the word from a previous context) must be performed.

In the seventeenth section of the second chapter of the *Mīmāṃsājaiminīya-sūtra* (2.1.36–37), [the author] formulates the following: "Is there no *anuṣaṅga* (supplying of ellipsis) or is there *anuṣaṅga*? The two [sentences] beginning with *achidreṇa* are the subordinates (*śeṣin*)."
The mantra "citpatistvā" is not to be supplied here for one who has no expectancy.

The status of being an instrument (*karaṇatva*) depends upon an action, and the action here is the single one expressed by "may he purify" (*punātu*). Therefore, through that [action] as its medium, the remainder of the mantra is attached as a supplement to all three mantras. In the *Jyotiṣṭoma*, within the section on initiation (*dīkṣā*), it is recited: "May the Lord of Thought (*citpati*) purify you; may the Lord of Speech (*vākpati*) purify you; may the divine Savitṛ purify you with a flawless filter, with the rays of the sun, the Vasu."
In that context, the remainder of the third mantra—the portion beginning with "acchidreṇa"—is not to be supplied (anuṣajyate) to the first and second mantras.
Why?
Because they are already complete in themselves (nirākāṅkṣatvāt).
For there is no expectancy for a supplement in these two complete sentences which are the principals— "May Citpati purify you" and "May Vākpati purify you"— this being the position reached,
we reply: "Even if there is no expectancy in the principals, there nevertheless exists an expectancy in the supplement."
For the status of being an instrument (karaṇatva) mentioned in the phrase "by means of the purifier, by means of the rays" requires an action;
and the action is this single one, "may he purify," which occurs in all three mantras.
Connected with that action, the remaining portion follows through the medium of the action even in the third mantra, despite its independence.
Likewise, it is appropriate that [the word] also applies to the two preceding [sentences].
Therefore, there is an *anuṣaṅga* (supplying of a word from a previous context).
(Regarding the section on non-attachment due to intervention, Sūtra 2.1.49:
Because of intervention, there should be no attachment. Jaimini 2.1.49.
START MJaiNy 2.1.38–39: He formulates the eighteenth (seventeenth) section—
Is there an ellipsis (*anuṣaṅga*) of the word "let them go" above [the mantra], or not? Because of its suitability in the phrase "that sacrificer," it exists there as before.

That singular number in the middle mantra, namely in the word *aṅgāni* (limbs), does not connect [with the plural *prāṇāḥ*]; because of that intervention, it is not carried over (*anuṣajyate*) to what follows either.
In the Agniṣomīya animal sacrifice, it is heard: “May your breath unite with the wind... (*saṃ te prāṇo vātena gacchatām*).
"May the limbs be united with the sacrificial deities; may the lord of the sacrifice be united with his blessing.
The meaning of this is: "O animal, may your vital breath (prāṇa) be joined with the external wind (vāta)."
"May your limbs today be joined with specific sacrifices;
may the lord of the sacrifice be joined with blessings.
In that context, because the prefix *sam* in the third mantra, "the lord of the sacrifice," requires a verbal action, [it must be supplied] from the first mantra.

Since the word "gacchatām" (let them go), being in the singular number, is capable of syntactically connecting with the word "yajñapati" (the lord of the sacrifice), and since it is present in the mind as before, the verb is supplied [to the latter] due to the existence of expectancy, proximity, and compatibility— this being the prima facie view— we reply: because it is incapable of connecting with the plural form "aṅgāni" (limbs) in the middle mantra, and because there is no mental proximity due to that intervention, there is no such supply of the verb.
Therefore, for the second and third mantras, the appropriate completion of the sentence must be supplied.
Thus ends the first quarter of the second chapter in the *Jaiminīyanyāyamālāvistara* by the venerable Mādhava.
[Now begins the second quarter of the second chapter] (In the first section concerning the distinction between the subsidiary apūrvas, the sūtra is as follows).

There is a difference in action due to a difference in words, because of the connection with what has been performed. (Jaimini 2.2.1) He introduces the first section of the second chapter: The first section of the second quarter begins: "There is a difference in action due to a difference in words, because of the connection with what has been performed. (Jaimini 2.2.1). Start MJaiNy 2.2.1-2.
In such cases as "he gives" (dadāti) and "he sacrifices" (yajati), is there identity or difference in the efficient force (bhāvanā)?
Because the verbal suffix (ākhyāta) is identical, there is unity; the difference in roots (dhātu) is irrelevant.
From that, it is heard that there is a distinction based on the difference in verbal roots (*dhātu*);
because they are colored by a single [act of] origination, the mental dispositions (*bhāvanā*) differ from one another.
Here, the verbs (*ākhyāta*) occurring within a single context, derived from different synonymous roots—such as *yajati*, [dadāti, dadhāti, juhoti, nirvapati]—[are distinct].
"he gives," "he offers oblations," and so forth, are the examples.
And these [injunctions] are heard as follows: "One should sacrifice with Soma," "He gives gold to the Ātreya," and "He offers the sacrificial fees.
Since the verbal suffix denoting the productive activity (*bhāvanā*) is singular in each of these, it is logical that the productive activity is one.
Nor does a difference in the verbal roots entail a difference in the productive activity.
Since the verbal root lacks the capacity to denote that [bhāvanā], it cannot be the motivator for it—this being the position reached, we reply:
let the finite verb (ākhyāta) alone be the motivator of the bhāvanā; and that finite verb is distinct for each verbal root.
For indeed, a single verbal suffix is not heard following multiple roots, nor is a single verb prescribed in grammar from a collection of roots.

Therefore, since multiple verbs arise as being colored by each individual root and thus express the productive urge (*bhāvanā*), the productive urges of sacrifice, giving, and oblation are distinct from one another. (1–2)
START MJaiNy 2.2.3:
Here he states the opinion of the Guru: "If it is argued that the scripture is non-different because the injunction is one, we say no."
"Due to the difference in the [sacrificial] materials (dhātu), the application (niyoga) necessarily differs when there is a difference in the treatise (śāstra).
This is the view of the Guru: that the subject matter of this chapter is not an inquiry into the difference of actions (karma), but rather an inquiry into the difference of treatises."

In this regard, the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is as follows: because the injunction (*niyoga*) expressed by the optative suffix (*liṅ*) in such expressions as "one should sacrifice," "one should give," and "one should offer oblations" is one and the same, and because verbal roots lack the capacity to express an injunction and are therefore not the primary motivators, the entire scripture constitutes a single injunction with respect to that single injunction.

Because the optative suffix (*liṅpratyaya*) differs for each root, and because it is impossible to prevent a difference even in the injunction (*niyoga*) qualified by that [suffix] due to the distinction between the various adjuncts (*anubandha*) of the root-meanings, the scripture (*śāstra*) following the injunction is distinct—this is the established conclusion (*siddhānta*). (MJaiNyC_2,2.3)

(Regarding the second section [adhikaraṇa] on the distinction of apūrva in the case of the fuel-sticks and so forth, the sūtra states: "In this way, the repeated mention of the same [act] would be purposeless, because there is no distinction. (Jaimini Sūtra 2.2.2)
The second section formulates the problem:
In such cases as "He offers the *samidh* oblations," is there unity or is there distinctness?
Since the verbal root and the suffix are one, there is unity; from what could there be distinctness?
"Due to repetition, there is a difference of action here; because it is a name, it is not an injunction regarding a quality.
Injunctional force appears from direct Vedic statement (śruti), while the status of a restatement (anuvāda) arises from proximity (saṃnidhi).

In the context of the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, it is heard in the scripture: "He offers to the Samidhs," "He offers to Tanūnapāt," "He offers to the Iḍas," "He offers to Barhis," and "He offers with the Svāhā-call."

In that case, when the word *yajati* (he sacrifices) is heard five times, there is no difference in the verbal root (*dhātu*), as there is in the previously mentioned words such as *yajati*, *dadāti*, and so forth, by which a difference in the productive operation (*bhāvanā*) might be suspected. Therefore, if it is argued that the unity of the productive operation is unavoidable due to the unity of the finite verb (*ākhyāta*), [we reply:]...
Not so;
for the distinction between actions is understood through the repetition of the verbal root *yajati* (to sacrifice).
If there were only a single action, the repetition would be purposeless.

Now, it might be argued: "By the first-occurring sentence, 'He sacrifices the *samidhs*,' a sacrifice named *samit* is enjoined; then, by the four subsequent occurrences of the word 'sacrifices' (*yajati*), those [sentences] refer back to that sacrifice and enjoin four optional alternatives—namely, the deities or substances beginning with *tanūnapāt*."
"Therefore, because it serves the purpose of restatement, repetition is not futile"—
this is not correct; for words such as *tanūnapāt* and so forth are names of sacrifices (*yāga-nāman*), and thus they cannot be injunctions of accessory qualities (*guṇa-vidhi*).
First of all, there is no injunction regarding a deity here,
because neither the dative case nor a secondary derivative (taddhita) is heard;
nor is there an injunction regarding a substance.

Because they lack the status of being in the nominative case (tṛtīyānta), the status of being names (nāmatva) is appropriate for those words ending in the accusative, just as in the case of "agnihotraṃ juhoti" and similar expressions. As for the claim that the four subsequent instances of the word *yajati* are merely restatements (anuvāda): [this is not so].
That is incorrect,
because they are prescriptive.
Just as in the case of "He offers the *samidhs*," the prescriptive nature of the word *yajati* (he offers) is understood through direct Vedic statement (*śruti*).
Likewise, in the case of the other four sentences as well, the status of being an injunction (*vidhitva*) is based on direct Vedic statement (*śruti*).
However, their status as restatements (*anuvādatva*) is understood through proximity (*saṃnidhi*) to the preceding statement, "He offers the *samidh* oblation.
And proximity is weaker than direct statement.

Furthermore, since it is impossible to enjoin again a sacrifice named *samit* that has already been enjoined by a preceding sentence, other sacrifices named *tanūnapāt* and so forth are being enjoined.
[Objection: If this is the case, then the distinction between rituals (*karmabheda*) results from the difference in names (*saṃjñābheda*), and not from repetition (*abhyāsa*).
If that were so, it would be conflated with the topic to be discussed later.
Not so;
for there is a difference between them.

In the example to be cited later, "Now this is the Jyotis," since the name is understood prior to the comprehension of the sacrifice, the name serves as a cause for the differentiation of the ritual acts. Here, however, once the sacrifices have been understood through the injunctive words containing the root *yajati*,
and their difference has been understood from repetition (*abhyāsa*), [the name functions differently].
Since distinct sacrifices require designations other than the name "samit," it is understood subsequently that *tanūnapāt* and the others are indeed names [of those sacrifices].
Therefore, repetition alone is the cause of differentiation here.

(Third Section: On the relationship of principal and subordinate among the Āghāra-libations, the Āgneya-offering, and others; Sūtras 3–8) "But the context [belongs] to the Full Moon sacrifice, because there is no mention of the form [of the subsidiaries]. (Jaimini 2.2.3) "And because a specific distinction is observed; for if all were equal, there would be no application [of the context]. (Jaimini 2.2.4)
But it is a quality, because of its connection with the Vedic text (Jaimini 2.2.5).

Or rather, there is an injunction of the qualities, because they are taught simultaneously; for when [the primary act] is enjoined, the qualities are taught as being for its sake, and thus each one would be prescribed [in relation to it] (Jaimini 2.2.6).
And the designation is likewise (Jaimini 2.2.7).
And because of the observation of an indicative mark (liṅga). Jaimini 2.2.8.
He formulates the third section as follows:

Thus, one who knows [this] should understand that the terms "Full Moon" (paurṇamāsī) and "New Moon" (amāvāsyā) refer either to other rites or to restatements of the previously mentioned collections [of rites].

There must be a distinct ritual action because of repetition; for the deity is certainly a substance, and it is not logical that there should be a restatement of what is already obtained from [the term] "vārtraghnī" and so forth.

Because of the statement regarding the fixed status of the *ājyabhāga* offerings as having "Vārtraghna" and so forth as their constituent parts, they do not have [independent] deities; likewise, the term "Paurṇa" (Full Moon) is merely a reference, and thus the triad associated with the Paurṇamāsī is established.
The purpose [of the word "also"] is the establishment of duality for the collection [of subsidiaries] through the two statements:
"He [performs] together" and "at the full moon"; thus, it applies to each triad [of rites].
In the injunction regarding the statements of the learned, there is a repetition of the injunction [of the primary acts] by means of the Āgneya and others;
that which is enjoined as the fruit is the principal, while the others are subordinate qualities.
This is recorded in the sacred tradition: "He who, knowing thus, sacrifices at the full moon," and "He who, knowing thus, sacrifices at the new moon."

In this context, a distinct ritual act (*karmāntara*) is enjoined by the term *yajati*, and the six previously mentioned sacrifices, such as the *Āgneya* and others, are not merely restated (*anūdyante*).

Furthermore, the *Āgneya* and other sacrifices connected with specific times are recorded in that very same section as follows: "The *Āgneya* cake on eight potsherds is never absent on the new moon and the full moon."
They two said, "O Agni and Soma, let us sacrifice with clarified butter alone, silently, at the full moon.
To them he gave this cake for Agni and Soma on eleven potsherds at the full moon;
[and he gave] curd for Indra at the new moon.

Regarding the statement, "The milk for Indra is [offered] on the new moon day," since this rite— enjoined by the sentence concerning those who possess knowledge— is distinct from these six previously mentioned rites beginning with the Āgneya,
the repetition of the injunction is justified according to the principle of the preceding section.
Nor is there an absence of substance and deity in another ritual action, because of the presence of the *dhruvājya* (the constant clarified butter);
for this very reason it has been said:
“The substance [of the *dhruvā*] is permanent and common; the deity is derived from the wording of the mantra.
Therefore, two formal sacrifices possessing form are enjoined separately.
Thus, the commonality of the *dhruvā* substance is heard in scripture: “Indeed, that clarified butter which is taken in the *dhruvā* is for the sake of every sacrifice.”
