The fact that the deity is established by the wording of the mantra (*māntravarṇikatva*) should be inferred in this way: “Therefore, the two *vārtraghna* verses are recited at the full moon, and the two *vṛdhanvatī* verses at the new moon. Thus, the two *vārtraghna* and the two *vṛdhanvatī* verses are prescribed for the rites associated with the two times respectively.
Among these, “Agni shall slay the Vṛtras” is one *vārtraghna* mantra.
"O Soma, you are the lord of the virtuous; you are the king and the slayer of Vṛtra"—this is another [verse].
Through these two recited verses, Agni and Soma are declared to be the deities of the full moon sacrifice (*paurṇamāsī*).
Likewise, through these two mantras recited within the text that contain the verbal root *vṛdh* (to increase), Agni and Soma are declared to be the deities of the new moon sacrifice (*amāvasyā*).
Because of these two—[the material] substance and the deity—possessing form, a distinct sacrifice is enjoined here.

If [these sentences] were mere restatements (anuvāda) of six sacrifices, then, since no other thing to be enjoined would be observed apart from that restatement, the "Vidvadvākya" would be purposeless.
Not only would it be purposeless, [but it would also contradict the established doctrine].
However, even the injunctions "One should sacrifice with the Paurṇamāsī on the full moon day" and "One should sacrifice with the Amāvāsyā on the new moon day" would become redundant;
nor do these serve as injunctions for the time [of the sacrifice].
"Since that [sacrifice] is enjoined by the very originative injunctions such as 'That which belongs to Agni' (yadāgneyaḥ),
[the sentence in question] will enjoin the time if it were a separate rite.
Therefore, it is a prescription for a separate rite"— this being the position reached, [we reply:]...
We reply: Let the substance be set aside for now;

however, a deity for the other rite intended to be enjoined cannot be found in any way whatsoever, because the two *vārtraghni* verses and the two *vṛdhanvatī* verses serve to designate the deities of the *ājyabhāga* offerings.

In the *Mantrakāṇḍa* of the *Āśvalāyana-śrautasūtra*, after the *sāmidhenī* verses, the *āvāhana-nigada*, and the *prayāja-mantras* have been recited, the two *vārtraghnī* and the two *vṛdhanvatī* verses are recited in the sequence of the two *ājyabhāgas* that occur immediately after the *prayājas*. Furthermore, indicative marks (*liṅga*) pertaining to Agni and Soma are found therein.
Consequently, by means of both indicative mark and sequence (*krama*), it is understood that these verses pertain to the *ājyabhāgas*.
As for the statement— "The *vārtraghnī* [verses] are at the full moon"— and so forth,
it merely declares the distribution of the two pairs of mantras (which are established by their indicative marks and sequence) between the two times for the two *ājyabhāga* offerings;
it does not, however, enjoin these as constituent parts of a new ritual action.

Therefore, because it lacks any mention of a material substance (*rūpa*), the statement of the learned [authorities] does not enjoin a separate ritual action; rather, it restates two groups consisting of three [offerings] each among the six previously mentioned [rites], such as the Āgneya and others.
Nor is there any impossibility of restating the sacrifices by means of the words *paurṇamāsī* and *amāvāsyā*, which denote specific times.
This is because the two sets of three sacrifices performed at those respective times are indicated;
nor is the restatement (anuvāda) purposeless,
for its purpose is the establishment of the duality of the two groups.

And once that [the six sacrifices] is established, the use of the dual number in the fruit-statement, “One desiring heaven should sacrifice with the Darśapūrṇamāsa,” is justified by the intention to refer to the six sacrifices.
As for what was said— that under the view of it being a restatement (anuvāda), the statements such as “on the full moon day” would be redundant—
that is incorrect.
Even though the prescription of time is not possible for a single triad, because there is a prescription for their simultaneous performance,

the simultaneous performance of the three— the Āgneya, the Upāṃśuyāja, and the Agnīṣomīya— which are prescribed for the time of the full moon, is enjoined by the word "paurṇamāsyām" (on the full moon), ending in the third case singular. The same applies elsewhere as well.

[Objection: "But even if the sentence concerning the learned man (*vidvadvākya*) does not enjoin a separate ritual action, it cannot be a mere restatement (*anuvādaka*), because it is admitted that it does not enjoin a sacrifice.

On the other hand, sentences such as ‘The cake on eight potsherds is for Agni’ (*āgneyo ’ṣṭākapālaḥ*) enjoin accessory qualities characterized by substance and deity, by way of restating sacrifices already enjoined. [Response: No.

That being the case, since it is impossible for multiple qualities to be enjoined by a single sentence, if each quality were enjoined separately, the fault of repetitive injunction (*vidhyāvṛtti*) would follow. However,
if the sentences concerning the *Āgneya* and other offerings are taken as injunctive, there is no fault of repetitive injunction because they function as qualified injunctions (*viśiṣṭavidhi*).
Therefore, the *vidvadvākya* (the sentence concerning the knower) is a restatement (*anuvāda*) of those [actions] enjoined by the sentences concerning the Āgneya and other offerings.

Furthermore, for one who, while accepting its status as a restatement, asserts that it is an injunction for a separate action (*karmāntara*), the relationship of subordinate and principal between the *prayāja*s and the like on the one hand, and the Āgneya and other offerings on the other, would not be established.
To explain: certain injunctions such as "He offers the *samidhs*" and "He pours the *āghāra*" are recorded in scripture as being devoid of connection with specific times.
There are other [rites] connected with specific times, such as: "The cake on eight potsherds for Agni at the new moon and at the full moon.
Since both these types [of rites] are under discussion, the sentence "One desiring heaven should sacrifice with the Darśapūrṇamāsa" must convey the connection of all of them with the fruit.
[Regarding] "with the Darśapūrṇamāsa..."
Thus, the dual number must be transformed into a plural;

for there are two distinct sets of rites prescribed in the sentences concerning the learned ones— the *prayāja*s and so forth, and the *āgneya* offerings and so forth— and because duality is impossible among these.

Furthermore, if all [the constituent acts] were connected with the fruit equally, then—just as in the case of the *iṣṭi*, animal sacrifice, and *soma* offerings belonging to the Rājasūya—the *prayāja* and other subsidiaries would not possess the status of being subordinate (*guṇabhāva*) due to their equal primacy.

In the absence of that subordination, they would lack the status of being auxiliary members (*anaṅgatva*), and consequently, there would be no extended application (*atideśa*) of them into modified forms (*vikṛti*) such as the Saurya sacrifice, just as there is none for the Āgneya and other primary rites.

However, under the view that [the sentence] is a restatement (*anuvāda*), the terms "New Moon" (*darśa*) and "Full Moon" (*pūrṇamāsa*) are applicable to the two triads because of their connection with specific times.

Furthermore, because the Āgneya and other sacrifices possess a dual number due to their being a collective whole, they alone are primary by virtue of their connection with the fruit; the Prayāja and other offerings, however, are subordinate. Thus, there is no fault whatsoever.
Therefore—the sentence containing the two "knowing" (vidvat) terms is merely a restatement (anuvādaka).
(Caturtha upāṃśuyājāpūrvatādhikaraṇa,
Sūtras 9–12) The Upāṃśuyāja should be like the Full Moon sacrifice. Or rather, it is a distinct injunction, because it is not previously established.
Because of the connection with the qualities; and because of the statement regarding the majority. (Jaimini Sūtra 2.2.11–12)
The fourth section formulates the problem:
Is this [phrase] "upāṃśuyājam" a restatement (anuvāda) here, or rather an injunction (vidhi)?
Because there is a clear injunction in the sentences concerning Viṣṇu and others, this [phrase] must be a restatement.
Since the mention of "jāmitva" (repetitiveness) occurs, there must be an injunction characterized by the *upāṃśu* (whispered) quality in the interval;
in that case, Viṣṇu and the others are merely explanatory statements (*arthavāda*), as their form is already established by the *dhrauvas* mantra.
This is recorded in the tradition: "Indeed, a repetitiveness is thereby created in the sacrifice."
Since he performs the *upāṃśuyāja* between the two successive *puroḍāśa* offerings,
Viṣṇu is to be sacrificed to in a whisper for the sake of non-repetition; Prajāpati is to be sacrificed to in a whisper for the sake of non-repetition.
"If Agni and Soma are to be sacrificed to in a low voice for the sake of non-redundancy"—
if it is argued that this is a restatement (anuvāda) of the triad of sacrifices enjoined in the passages concerning Viṣṇu and the others,
it is not so.

Since the defect of *jāmitva* (monotony) caused by the lack of interval between the two *puroḍāśa* offerings dedicated to Agni and Agnīṣoma is introduced at the beginning of the passage, something is intended to be enjoined in the interval between the two *puroḍāśas*.
For in the sentences concerning Viṣṇu and the others, nothing qualified by the quality of being "in the interval" (*antarāla*) is perceived as the object of injunction;
however, since that [quality] is perceived in the preceding sentence, that sentence is injunctive.
Nor should it be suspected that the term "yajati" here is a statement in the present tense (*vartamānāpadeśa*),
because the fifth verbal suffix (*pañcamalakāra*) is employed.
Since the quality of being whispered (*upāṃśutva*) is a qualification— just like the intermediate time— the action qualified by that [quality] constitutes the context for the Upāṃśuyāja.

This being the case, once the action characterized by these two qualities has been enjoined by the first sentence, the sentences concerning Viṣṇu and the others would function as explanatory eulogies (*arthavāda*).
Furthermore, one should not suspect that there is an injunction of a deity here by way of restating the sacrifice already enjoined;
for the discourse begins with the defect of "sameness" (*jāmitva*) which must be remedied.

Furthermore, because of the conclusion through the resolution of non-repetition (*ajāmitva*), there is the perception of a single unified meaning for the entire great sentence (mahāvākya) beginning with "It is indeed repetitive" and ending with "for the sake of non-repetition.
Indeed, a multiplicity of things to be enjoined is not possible within a single sentence;
nor is there an absence of a material substance for the *upāṃśuyāja* sacrifice which is intended to be enjoined here.
Because that [material] belongs to Dhruva;
nor is there an absence of a deity,
since the three deities are understood as alternatives through the Vaiṣṇava, Prājāpatya, and Āgnīṣomīya mantras recited in the sequence of the Upāṃśuyāja across various Vedic branches.
Therefore, "he sacrifices" (yajati) is the injunctive statement.
(Section on the novelty of the Āghāra and Agnihotra, Sūtras 13–16):
The Āghāra and Agnihotra [are independent acts] because they lack a [previously known] form;
because of the connection with a specific name. Jaimini 2.2.13–14.
And because it is not the subject under discussion.

(Jaimini 2.2.15) On the contrary, it is an injunction, because the meaning of the word is intended for performance; therefore, its repetition in proximity [to the primary injunction] is for the purpose of indicating a subordinate quality. (Jaimini 2.2.16)
The fifth section formulates [the following]: Is the sentence concerning the *agnihotra* and the *āghāra* an explanatory restatement (*anuvāda*) or an injunction (*vidhi*)?

However, because it lacks a specific ritual form (*arūpatva*), that which was already stated by the sentences regarding curd (*dadhi*) and "upwards" (*ūrdhva*) is here restated. (Jaimini Sūtra 2.2.13)
If the substratum possessing the quality (*guṇin*) were already established, then curd and the like could not be a quality, and the qualified entity (*viśiṣṭatā*) would be defective.

Therefore, since the form [of the action] is established by both the word "curd" (*dadhi*) and the word "offering" (*juhoti*), this is an injunction of the substratum possessing the quality (*guṇividhi*).
This is handed down in the tradition: "One offers the Agnihotra," "One offers with curd," and "One offers with milk."
This other traditional teaching is as follows: "He pours the base-oblation," "He pours upwards," and "He pours straight.
Among these, the Agnihotra statement is a restatement (anuvāda) of the collection of rites enjoined by the statements regarding curds and so forth;
and the Āghāra statement is a restatement of that which is enjoined by the statements regarding "upwards" and so forth.
If it is argued: "But these two sentences do not enjoin a ritual action;
why?
Because the form of a sacrifice, characterized by a material substance and a deity, is absent."
In this regard, it must be stated: is only a quality enjoined by the sentence concerning curd and so forth, or is an action qualified by a quality enjoined?
Not the first.

In your view, however, since sentences such as "The Agnihotra [is to be performed]" lack the status of being injunctions for ritual action (*karma-vidhi*), no substratum possessing qualities (*guṇin*) is established; consequently, it is impossible to enjoin a mere quality preceded by a reference to that substratum.
In the second case, there would be an excessive complexity of injunction (*vidhi-gaurava*), and that is improper when an alternative course is available.
Therefore, the sentence concerning the Agnihotra and other such rites is an injunction for ritual action (*karma-vidhi*).
In that context, the material substance (*dravya*) is obtained from sentences concerning curd and so forth,
while the deity (*devatā*), however, is derived from the wording of the mantras (*māntravarṇikī*).
In the case of the *āghāra* offering as well, the substance and the deity must likewise be inferred.
(Section on the Apūrva nature of the Animal and Soma sacrifices, Sūtras 17–20):

In the context of the Animal and Soma sacrifices, there is an injunction regarding the substance; for the connection with the substance would otherwise be purposeless, as it is not for the sake of a subordinate quality. (Jaimini 2.2.17) And the preparatory rites are not injunctive [of the sacrifice]. (Jaimini 2.2.18)

Due to that distinction, there would be repetition of the action because of the separateness of the substance; for otherwise, the distinction [of the action] would be purposeless due to the substance being subordinate. (Jaimini 2.2.19) But the consecration (*saṃskāra*) would not be distinct, because it is for the sake of another and because the substance is subordinate.
(Jaimini 2.2.20)
The sixth section formulates the following problem:

Are "he sacrifices" (yajati) and "he immolates" (ālabhati) restatements (anuvāda) of what is already enjoined by "he takes up" (gṛhṇāti) and "he cuts off" (avadyati), or are they themselves injunctions? MJaiNy_2.2.15.
Since there is no prior statement (purovāda) to support it, the mention of the *yajati* and *ālabhati* is not a restatement (*anuvāda*); therefore, it is an injunction (*vidhi*).
The [mention of] *brahmaṇe* is a refinement of the Soma, while [the mention of] *avadāna* is a refinement of the animal victim. The scripture states: "One should sacrifice with Soma. (Soma-yajeta).
In that regard, scriptural injunctions such as "He draws the cup for Indra and Vāyu," "He draws the cup for Mitra and Varuṇa," and so forth, are also heard.
Likewise, it is heard in scripture: "One should immolate an animal dedicated to Agni and Soma."
In that regard, scriptural passages such as "He cuts from the heart first,
then from the tongue,
then from the chest," and so forth, have also been heard.
In this context, sacrifices are enjoined by the sentences beginning with "indravāyu" (for Indra and Vāyu),

because the deities such as Indra and Vāyu and the substance consisting of Soma juice are understood through the nominal stems (*prātipadika*) "indravāyu" and so forth, along with their respective suffixes.
The collection of these sacrifices, which are enjoined by the sentences of extraction (*grahaṇa*), is restated (*anūdyate*) by the sentence "one should sacrifice with Soma" (*somena yajeta*).
Likewise, in the sentences concerning the portions (*avadāna*), substances such as the heart and so forth are heard;
therefore, sacrifices qualified by those substances are enjoined therein.
By way of restating that [fact], the deity in the form of Agni-Soma is enjoined in the sentence concerning the immolation of the animal (*paśvālambha*).

Therefore, when it is argued that "the collection of sacrifices enjoined by the sentences regarding the portions (*avadāna*) is restated by the sentence ‘one should immolate the animal’"—to this we reply: for a restatement (*anuvāda*) occurs only when there is a prior injunction (*purovāda*).
Furthermore, there is no prior statement (purovāda) here;
for the meaning understood from the injunction "One should sacrifice with Soma" is not perceived in the sentences concerning the drawing of the cups (grahaṇa),
since the act of drawing is not the act of sacrificing.
Nor is it to be suspected that the *rasa* expressed by the secondary derivative suffix (*taddhita-pratyaya*) refers to the Soma plant;
nor should one suspect that the secondary derivative suffix, being prescribed in the sense of a pronoun (*sarvanāman*), denotes the subject under discussion (*prakṛta*) but not the *rasa*.

Because it is the *rasa* (essence) itself that is the subject under discussion in the statement, "He takes [it] with a stream," so too, the meaning understood from the injunction "One should immolate the animal" is not what is understood in the sentences concerning the portions (*avadāna*). Therefore,

since there is no possibility of a restatement (*anuvāda*) due to the absence of a prior statement (*pūrvavāda*), two distinct ritual acts are enjoined by the verbs *yajati* (he sacrifices) and *ālabhati* (he immolates).
By the sentences concerning the taking [of the soma], a refinement of the soma qualified by a deity is enjoined;
and by the sentences concerning the cutting [of portions], a refinement of the animal victim is enjoined.
(Regarding the seventh section on the distinction of rites based on number:
Sūtra) Because they reside separately, there should be a distinction of rites by virtue of the number. Jaimini 2.2.21.
The seventh section formulates the problem:
Regarding the statement "three oblations," is there unity of action or is there a distinction?
There is unity because the verb is uttered once; the number applies by repetition, as in the case of the *prayāja* offerings. (Mīmāṃsā-jaiminīya-nyāyamālā-vistara 2.2.17)
The mere mention [of the number] is not our authority for [assuming] plurality of action;
rather, the state of being eleven in the *prayāja* arises from repetition, due to the absence of any other way [to account for the number].

Regarding the statement, "Seventeen animals dedicated to Prajāpati," the author of the Bhāṣya states that an inquiry is necessary here, because in the preceding case, the triad of actions was clearly evident. (Mīmāṃsā Nyāya Bindu 2.2.19)
Due to the intervention of the deity, there is non-difference of form with respect to the many cattle possessed;
therefore, the action is one, and number here does not pertain to the ritual act itself.

The final [element] of that secondary derivative (taddhita) meaning which is already connected with a deity is the connection with plurality; the distinction of its action is by means of the number of forms. "He offers three oblations," so it is heard in the scripture.
In this context, the verbal root "juhoti" (he offers) is not repeated— as is the case with "samidho yajati" and so forth— but is rather recorded only once;
therefore, this is a single ritual action.
However, the number three must be understood as resulting from the repetition of that very same action;
just as the number eleven in the *prayāja* offerings is accounted for by the repetition of the five *prayāja*s themselves, so it is here— this being the position reached.
We reply: Is this verbal form (ākhyāta) a means of proof for the unity of action independently of other words, or is it [a means of proof] when connected with other words?
Not the first.
Because a mere word, being only a part of a sentence, lacks the capacity to produce valid knowledge.
In the second case— the view that the verb qualified by the number three indicates a plurality of objects—
it is difficult to achieve the number eleven for the *prayāja* offerings without repetition, since they are already restricted to the number five.

In this case, however, there is a disparity because, prior to the injunction, there is no restriction of the action to the number one. The author of the Bhāṣya does not accept this example cited by the author of the Vṛtti;

for since the word *āhuti* (oblation), which denotes the action, is qualified by the word *tri* (three), the plurality of actions is made explicit, and thus the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) cannot arise.
The illustration here is as follows: "He sacrifices seventeen animals dedicated to Prajāpati.

In this case, through the derivation of the secondary nominal suffix (*taddhita*), [the term] *prājāpatyāḥ* means "those animals whose deity is Prajāpati. Although plurality is indicated, the animals constitute a single substance (*dravya*).
Consequently, because of the unity of the substance and the unity of the deity, the form of the sacrifice is undifferentiated; thus, this is a single ritual action (*karman*).
As for the number "seventeen," it resides in the substance of the animal,
and not in the action as was the case with the number three cited previously.
Therefore, when it is argued that "this does not result in a difference in the ritual action," we reply:
here, one first derives the nominal stem ending in a secondary suffix (*taddhita*) as "prājāpatyaḥ" (belonging to Prajāpati), meaning "that animal whose deity is Prajāpati";

subsequently, when the desire arises to express the objecthood and plurality of that animal—qualified by the deity Prajāpati—which is the referent of the nominal stem ending in the secondary suffix, [the dual suffix is produced].
These are the plural forms of the second case (accusative).

In that regard, even at the time of the derivation of the secondary suffix (*taddhita*), there is no syntactic connection with the second case itself, which occurs first; how much less so can there be a connection with the plural number, which occurs later?

This being the case, by the nominal stem ending in a secondary derivative (*taddhita*)— namely, *prājāpatyaḥ*— the form of the sacrifice is presented as consisting of a single animal substance and accompanied by a single deity.
The plural number is used to indicate the multiplicity of such forms,
and the specific quality of that multiplicity is indicated by the term *saptadaśaḥ* ("seventeen").
Therefore, in this case, there is a distinction of rites based on the number. This being so,

it is logically consistent that what will be stated in the eighth [book]— namely, that the seventeen animals constitute a modification (*vikṛti*) of the group of eleven animals (*ekādaśinī*)— is established.
(Aṣṭama Adhikaraṇa: On the Distinction of Actions Based on Names;
Sūtra) And the name [is a means of differentiation], because of its connection with the originative injunction. Jaimini 2.2.22.
The eighth section formulates the following:
Now, regarding the passage "atha eṣa jyotiḥ" (Now this is the Jyotis), is it a quality or a separate rite?
It is a quality, consisting of the gift of a thousand [cows], because the Jyotiṣṭoma is being referred to [as the subject]. (MJaiNy 2.2.22)
The word *atha* (now) refers to what has been interrupted in the context; the word *etat* (this) would denote that which follows.
Here, by means of a new name, there is indeed a different ritual action, just as [a number indicates a different sacrifice].
"Now this Jyotis... [etc.]
Now this Viśvajyotis sacrifice, then this Sarvajyotis sacrifice— it is heard in scripture that one should perform the sacrifice with this one, for which a thousand [cows] are the sacrificial fee.

If it is argued that the *jyotiṣṭoma*, which is the subject under discussion here, is referred to by the words "this is the light" (*eṣa jyotiḥ*), and that a quality characterized by the giving of a thousand [cows] is enjoined with respect to it—[we reply: no;
because the subject under discussion, the *jyotiṣṭoma*, has been interrupted by the word "now" (*atha*).
Nor should it be said that, this being the case, the use of the pronoun "this" (*etad*) in the statement "this is the light" (*ayaiṣa jyotiḥ*) would be untenable.
Since the word *etad* (this), which denotes what is proximate, can refer to both what is past-proximate and what is future-proximate,
and since the meaning of the word *jyotis* (light) is that which is future-proximate,
this word *jyotis*, not referring back to something past, designates some new ritual action because it functions as a novel name (*saṃjñā*).
Therefore, just as in the previous case the action was differentiated by number, here too the action is differentiated by name;
this same principle is to be seen in the case of the two terms *viśvajyotis* and *sarvajyotis* as well.
(Regarding the ninth section, concerning the differentiation of rituals based on the differentiation of deities, there is the sūtra:
"And [the mention of] qualities [constitutes a separate ritual], because when there is a connection with a new [result], the two sentences are equal. Jaimini 2.2.23.

The ninth section formulates the problem: "In the injunction 'vājibhyo vājinam' (ghee for the Vājins), is there a subordinate element (guṇa) or a distinct ritual act? It is a subordinate element, because the deities are restated [from the previous rite], and thus conjunction or option would otherwise result. (Mīmāṃsā-jaiminīya-sūtra 2.2.24)

Because the *āmikṣā* (curd-mixture) is prescribed as the primary material for the production [of the sacrifice], it is stronger; therefore, the *vājina* (whey), being a subordinate quality (*guṇa*), cannot enter into that [same] rite but must be understood as constituting a different ritual action having the *vājins* as its deities. [Commentary: "One pours curds into heated milk... (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 6.5.10.4). In this context, the *āmikṣā* is produced by the very act of pouring curds into boiled milk; thus, it is established by the originative injunction (*utpatti-śiṣṭa*) and is consequently more powerful. Since the *vājina* is merely a secondary quality (*guṇa*) remaining after the *āmikṣā* has been extracted, it cannot be subsumed under that same ritual action. Instead, it must be construed as a distinct ritual act dedicated to the *vājins*. This is because the presence of two incompatible materials—boiled milk and curds—within a single offering would result in a contradiction regarding the nature of the substance to be offered. Therefore, the *vājina* establishes a separate ritual procedure.
It is heard in scripture: "That is the *āmikṣā* for the Viśvedevas; the *vājina* for the Vājins.
*Āmikṣā* is a mass of milk that has become solidified.
*Jalam* means *vājinam*.
In that context, those *Viśvedevas* who were mentioned as partakers of the *āmikṣā* substance are referred to by the term "*vājibhyaḥ*."
"Vāja" means food, and it exists for them in the form of curdled milk (*āmikṣā*), because that is what produces it.
Having referred back to those [deities], a subordinate element (*guṇa*) consisting of the substance *vājina* is enjoined.
As for that substance, it follows that it must either be combined with the substance of the curdled milk or be an alternative to it—this being the prima facie view (*pūrva-pakṣa*).

We reply: Since the Vaiśvadeva sacrifice is already occupied by the curd (*āmikṣā*) substance prescribed at the time of its origination, there is no room for the whey (*vājina*) substance prescribed as a subsequent rule; therefore, the whey brings about a different deity for the meaning of the word *vājin*.
Consequently, because the form characterized by the substance and the deity is distinct, it constitutes a separate ritual action.
(Regarding the section on the unity of action due to the non-specification of ten distinct substances, the sūtra states:
"But when the word denotes an action that lacks a quality, then a quality would be understood therein. (Jaimini Sūtra 2.2.24)
The tenth section formulates the problem:
"In the case of the curd-offering (*dadhi-homa*), is it a separate rite, or is it a subordinate element (*guṇa*) as in the previous cases?
Because the Agnihotra is devoid of such a substance, curd and the like are properly regarded as subordinate elements. (Mīmāṃsā-jaiminīya-sūtra 2.2.26)

It is heard in scripture: "He offers curd. In this regard, according to the previous principle, it is understood that the act consisting of the offering of curd is a ritual action distinct from the previously mentioned primary rite, "He performs the Agnihotra," just as in the preceding case the rite was differentiated by the substance *vājina*.
If it is argued that it is likewise by means of the substance curd, we say no,
because of the disparity.
For example, the Vaiśvadeva sacrifice is already occupied by the quality of *āmikṣā*.
Likewise, the Agnihotra is not already occupied by other qualities;
on the contrary, because it is devoid of qualities, it requires a quality.
Therefore, this is an injunction of a quality (guṇavidhi).
The same should be understood regarding injunctions such as "one offers with milk.

Since all substances such as milk, curd, and so forth are equally authoritative as being prescribed for an already established rite (*utpannaśiṣṭa*), and because the Agnihotra can be accomplished by each individual substance, there is an option (*vikalpa*) among them, just as in the case of rice and barley.
(Regarding the eleventh section, on the fruitfulness of substances such as curd, Sūtras 25–26:
"But because of the mention of a fruit, it must be a ritual act, since a fruit is connected with a ritual act" (Jaimini 2.2.25).
"But because of the inequality of the two sentences, it should be understood as a subordinate element of that [act]" (Jaimini 2.2.26).
He formulates the eleventh topic:
"That which says, 'One desiring sensory power should offer curd,' that is distinct [from the primary injunction]."
Or rather, the action is differentiated as a subordinate factor (guṇa), because the meaning of the verbal root has become the primary result.
Due to the heaviness of the sense of possession (*matvartha*) and other such factors, there is no action other than this that leads to the fruit;
rather, when a quality (*guṇa*) is to be enjoined, the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) is restated (*anūdyate*) because it has already been enjoined elsewhere.
In the Vedic text it is heard: "One desiring sensory power should offer oblations with curds" (*dadhnendriyakāmasya juhuyāt*).
This, therefore, is a ritual action other than the original Agnihotra;
however, there is no injunction here.
Why?

If it is argued that because the result stated as "for one desiring sensory power" (*indriyakāmasya*) cannot be accomplished from the mere substance alone without the meaning of the verbal root (the action), [the word *homena* must be taken as an injunction of a separate act]—it is not so; for if a separate act were enjoined, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of a possessive indication (*matvarthalakṣaṇā*), namely: "one should effect sensory power by means of a sacrifice possessing curd."
In the case of an injunction for an action qualified by an accessory, there would be prolixity;
furthermore, it would entail the abandonment of the subject matter under discussion and the introduction of something not previously mentioned.
Therefore, it is the accessory alone that is enjoined for the sake of the result.
Although it is established by the injunction "He offers with curd" (*dadhnā juhoti*), nevertheless, the connection with a fruit [of action] is not established.
If it is argued that a fruit is impossible when the meaning of the verbal root is not manifest, we say: no.

Because the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) enjoined in the injunction "He performs the *agnihotra*" is what is being restated (*anūdyamāna*). (Mīmāṃsā-jaiminīya-nyāyamālā-vistara 2.2.27–28)

(Regarding the section on whether the Vāravantīya and other rites constitute separate acts in the twelfth [pāda], the sūtra states: "In the case of equal [elements], it should be connected with the ritual act. Jaimini 2.2.27.
The twelfth section formulates the problem:

"Having performed the Agniṣṭut sacrifice, having indeed applied the Vāravantīya sāman to the Revatī verses"—this is heard in scripture for the sake of attaining the fruit of cattle. (Mīmāṃsā-jaiminīya-nyāyamālā-vistara 2.2.29)
The ritual action possesses the quality of Revatī and so forth either separately or as a quality as before;
it is known as the connection between the Revatī verses and the Vāravantīya chant, and it bestows cattle.
In this case, if there were a connection of the *sāman* with both the fruit and the action, there would be a syntactical split (*vākya-bheda*).
Therefore, another action, conjoined with the previously mentioned quality, is enjoined for the sake of the fruit:
"The *trivṛt-agniṣṭut* is an *agniṣṭoma*; having performed the *ekaviṃśa-agniṣṭoma-sāman* upon the *vāyavyā* verses, one desiring the status of a Brahmin... [should sacrifice].

In proximity to the injunction "one should sacrifice," it is heard: "Having made the Vāravantīya the Agniṣṭoma-sāman upon these very Revatī verses, one desiring cattle should indeed sacrifice with this.
The meaning of this is as follows: there is a certain one-day rite (ekāha) named Agniṣṭut, which is a modification (vikṛti) of the Agniṣṭoma.
And because it is associated with the *trivṛt* soma-stotra during the *pṛṣṭha* laud, it is called "the *trivṛt*";
furthermore, because it takes the form of the *agniṣṭoma* among the seven soma-terminuses (*saṃsthās*)—namely, the *agniṣṭoma*, *uktha*, and so forth—it is also called "the *agniṣṭoma*.
In the archetype (*prakṛti*), the *yajñāyajñīya* sāman is chanted over the *ārbhavapavamāna* at the third pressing (*tṛtīyasavana*).
And because the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice is completed by means of that *sāman*, it is called the "Agniṣṭoma-sāman.

In the archetype (*prakṛti*), that *sāman* is sung upon the verses addressed to Agni, beginning with "yajñāyajñā vo agnayaḥ. However, in this Agniṣṭut sacrifice, that *sāman* must be sung upon verses addressed to Vāyu by one who desires spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*).
And that [Vāravantīya] is endowed with the twenty-one-fold stoma, just as in the archetype.
However, for one desiring cattle, it is stated: "One should sing the Vāravantīya Sāman upon the Revatī verses, beginning with *revatīr naḥ sadhamādaḥ*.
In that case, there is a connection between the Revatī verses and the Sāman named Vāravantīya.
Thus, this [agniṣṭut] is enjoined for the sake of the fruit of cattle;

for it is the agniṣṭut that is presented by the word "etasya" (of this), which refers back to the subject under discussion, and by the particle "eva" (only/exclusively), which serves to exclude others.
Just as in the previous section, when curd was prescribed as an accessory for the *agnihotra* which is already established as having the sense-organs as its fruit, so it is here.
This being the position reached, we reply: the illustrative example is dissimilar.
The fact that curd is a producer of the oblation (*homa*) does not need to be made known by the scripture.
Since that [connection] can be understood from common worldly experience,
there is no syntactical split (*vākyabheda*) in the case where only the connection with the result is to be taught by the scripture.

Here, however, because both the fact that the *vāravantīya* chant— based on the *revatī* verses and the *udgītha*— is a means for the *agniṣṭut* rite and its being a means for the result must be taught by a single scriptural statement, a syntactical split is unavoidable.
Therefore, a different ritual action characterized by the aforementioned qualities, namely the *paśuphalaka* (the animal-sacrifice), is enjoined here.
Both the word "this" (*etad*) and the particle "only" (*eva*) are to be construed as referring to this distinct ritual action being enjoined.
(Thirteenth Section: On the Unity of Desire in the *Saubhara* and the *Nidhana*;
Sūtras 28–29) In the *Saubhara*, because of the mention of "man" (*puruṣa*), the connection with desire pertains to the *nidhana*.

(Jaimini 2.2.28) Or rather, because the entire [sāman] has its desire already stated, the mention of desire regarding that [the *saubhara*] would be for the purpose of the *nidhana*; it is a restatement. (Jaimini 2.2.29)
Starting with *Mīmāṃsā-jaiminīya-sūtra* 2.2.32–35,
the thirteenth section (adhikaraṇa) is formulated as follows:
"The Saubhara chant has been prescribed for those desiring rain, food, and heaven."
The *nidhanas* are also [the means] for rain and so forth, through the syllables *hīṣ*, *ūrg*, and *gū*.

Is another fruit, such as rain and so forth, [the result] of the Īśa and other [melodies], or is the *nidhana* restricted to the *saubhara* when it is connected with a specific fruit that has been mentioned?
A different result is stated in the fourth [case]: "For one desiring rain, [the word] *hīṣ*.
Thus, the fruit of the *saubhara* chant is augmented by its connection with *hīṣ*, which is for the sake of rain.
There is no difference [in the result] for those desiring rain, food, or other things, because of recognition (*pratyabhijñā*).
Even though there is a restriction regarding the fourth [note], this is appropriate because it is for that purpose (*tādarthya*).
"One who desires rain, one who desires food, or one who desires heaven—let him praise with the *saubhara* chant."
Having recited, "All desires indeed [are fulfilled] in the Saubhara," it is further recited: "One should employ 'hīṣ' as the *nidhana* for one desiring rain;
'ūrj' for one desiring food;
and 'ū' for one desiring heaven."
*Saubhara* is a specific *sāman*.
A *nidhana* is the final section of a *sāman* consisting of five or seven parts.

Within that *nidhana*, specific elements such as *hīṣ* and others are enjoined to produce results other than rain and so forth—the results of rain and so forth which are achieved through the praise (*stotra*) accomplished by the *Saubhara* *sāman*.
Why?
Because in the injunctive sentences for *hīṣ* and so forth, the dative case is heard in such expressions as "for one desiring rain" (*avṛṣṭikāmāya*).
Expressing that purpose (*tādarthye*), the dative case indicates that *hīṣ* and the other elements are subordinate to the person who desires rain and the like.
And this status of being a subsidiary (śeṣatva) is possible only when there is the means to achieve a fruit desired by the person.
Consequently, there would be two rains as the fruits of both the *saubhara* chant and the specific *hīṣ* finale;
from the combination of these two, a great rain results—this being the position reached [by the opponent].
We reply: he who desires rain and so forth in the injunction for the *saubhara* chant is recognized as the very same person in the injunction for the *hīṣ* syllable and others.
Therefore, those very results such as rain that constitute the fruit of the *saubhara* are restated (anūdyante) in the sentences concerning the *hīṣ* and other syllables.
Thus, there is no other result.

Now, it might be argued: "Since there is no new, distinct result, and since the *hīṣ* and other syllables are already obtained in the *saubhara* chant through the mere study of various Vedic branches, this injunction is purposeless."
That is not so;

for, since there is no fixed rule regarding which of the *hīṣ* and other *nidhanas* should be used among those three who desire the three respective fruits, the injunction serves the purpose of restriction (*niyamārthatva*).

As for its being for that purpose (*tādarthya*), even though there is no separate fruit [for the *hīṣ* etc.], it is appropriate because the *hīṣ* and others are restricted as means within the *saubhara* chant—which is already established by the *saubhara* sentence itself—as a producer of fruits such as rain.
Therefore, this is a rule for the restriction of a specific *nidhana*.
Thus ends the second quarter of the second chapter in the *Jaiminīyanyāyamālāvistara* by the venerable Mādhava.

Is it another ritual action connected with the Rathantara and other [sāmans], or is it a subordinate element (guṇa)?
It is another [action] distinct from the previous one associated with the Gāyatrī and others, because of its differentiation by means of these qualities.
In the context of the word *soma*, which refers to the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, the precedence of the cups (*grahāgratva*) is a subordinate quality (*guṇa*), and there is mutual exclusion between them.
In the context of the Jyotiṣṭoma, it is heard [in scripture]: "If the Soma sacrifice should have the Rathantara as its *sāman*, one should draw the cups beginning with those for Indra and Vāyu."
"If [the sacrificer] has the Bṛhat-sāman, [the cups] should have the Śukra at the front; if he has the Jagat-sāman, [they] should have the Āgrayaṇa at the front.
In this context, by the word "soma," a sacrifice performed with the *soma* plant as its means is denoted.
And at that sacrifice, on the day of the pressing during the *pṛṣṭha-stotra*, the *sāmans* named Rathantara, Bṛhat, and Jagat are prescribed as alternatives.
The Rathantara arises from the *yoni* verse "abhi tvā śūra";
the Bṛhat arises from the [verse] "tvāmiddhi havāmahe."
That which arises from a verse in the Jagatī metre is the Jagat [Sāman].
It belongs to Indra;
it is for the Āyus and the Maitrāvaruṇa.
The Āśvina cup, the Śukra cup, the Manthin cup, and the Āgrayaṇa cup.
The cups named Ukthya, Dhruva, and so forth, are drawn during the morning pressing (prātaḥsavana).
They are called *grahas* because the Soma juice is drawn (*grahaṇa*) into wooden vessels.
In the version of the Soma sacrifice where it is accompanied by the *rathaṃtara* chant, the Aindravāyava cup is to be drawn first among these cups;
in the version accompanied by the *bṛhat* chant, the Śukra cup is first.
The meaning of the subject sentence is that, in the view that it possesses the *jagatsāman*, the *āgrayaṇa* cup is the first.
In that context, the *jyotiṣṭoma* under discussion is already endowed with the *gāyatra* and other *sāmans*;
therefore, the qualities such as the *rathantara* and so forth are mentioned here for the purpose of excluding that [standard configuration].

Therefore, when it is argued that "other distinct rites endowed with qualities such as the Aindravāyava [cup] are enjoined here," we reply: by the word *soma* used in the statement, "If the Soma sacrifice should have the Rathantara-sāman," and by the context (*prakaraṇa*), it is the Jyotiṣṭoma that is presented here.
Once that [Jyotiṣṭoma] has been assigned [as the substratum], the quality of being the foremost of the cups (*grahāgratva*) as previously stated is enjoined.
Furthermore, it is not possible to exclude the Jyotiṣṭoma by way of a restatement (*anuvāda*) of qualities such as the *rathaṃtara*,

because although it possesses the *gāyatra* and other *sāmans* in the morning libation (*prātaḥsavana*) and so forth, it also possesses the connection with the *rathaṃtara* and others in the *pṛṣṭha-stotra*.
If it is asked, "What then is excluded?
we reply: it is the mutual exclusion of the Rathantara, Bṛhat, and Jagat [sāmans].
The Rathantara and others are optional alternatives for the Pṛṣṭha-stotra.
In that case, by means of the restatement (*anuvāda*) of the *rathaṃtara*, the other two sides are excluded;

Therefore, it is an injunction of a subordinate quality (*guṇavidhi*).
Now, it may be argued that the Jyotiṣṭoma under discussion is the archetype (*prakṛti*) for other Soma sacrifices;

The statement regarding the *āgrayaṇa* being first does not enjoin a separate ritual action.

The term "kingdom" (*rājya*) is applied figuratively to the protection of subjects by Brāhmaṇas and Vaiśyas.
