The fourth section formulates the problem: "When it is said, 'One desiring heaven should sacrifice with the Dākṣāyaṇa-yajña,' is this a separate ritual action, or is it an accessory (guṇa) prescribed for the attainment of the fruit in the Darśa and other sacrifices already mentioned? (MJaiNy 2.3.10).
Because this quality (*guṇa*) is not well-known [as a distinct entity], there is a difference of action here due to the name;
the quality, established by etymology and supplementary statement, is called "repetition" (*āvṛtti*), and it is not a mere name.
In the context of the *Darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices, it is heard in scripture: "One desiring heaven should sacrifice with the *Dākṣāyaṇayajña*."

In this regard, if it is argued that— since no quality denoted by the word *dākṣāyaṇa* is well-known in the world, and because, like the word *udbhid*, it stands in grammatical apposition with the verb root and is therefore the name of a ritual action—
it must be an injunction for a different ritual action under a new name, as in the case of "Now this is the Jyotis" and so forth— [we reply]: No,
because the word *dākṣāyaṇa* denotes repetition (*āvṛtti*).
And that [meaning] is understood either from the etymology of the word or from the remainder of the sentence.
For instance: "ayanam" (going) denotes repetition;
"these belong to Dakṣa, thus they are Dākṣas."
"Their path" (*teṣām ayana*) is its etymological derivation.

*Dakṣa* means energetic; that is to say, one who is not indolent in returning again and again. The meaning of the word *dākṣāyaṇa* is the repetition of those [sacrificial] performances belonging to such a person.
Thus, the sacrifice under discussion, consisting of the New and Full Moon sacrifices, when joined with repetition (*āvṛtti*), becomes the *Dākṣāyaṇa-yajña*.
The manner of this repetition is understood from supplementary scriptural statements (*vākyaśeṣa*) such as, "One should sacrifice at two full moons; one should sacrifice at two new moons."

Therefore, since the meaning is well-established—just as in the case of curd and other such substances—this is an injunction regarding an accessory called *āvṛtti* (repetition) for the sake of attaining the fruit of heaven, pertaining to the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices which are already established in context;
it is not, like *udbhid* and others, a name for a ritual action.
The same should be understood in the case of the statement: "One desiring cattle should sacrifice with the *sākaṃprasthāpya*."
In the New Moon sacrifice (*amāvāsyā-yāga*), having prepared two milkings each, one proceeds with the simultaneous setting out of the four jars of curds and milk; this is the *sākaṃprasthāpya*.
The sacrifice connected with that [procedure] is the *sākaṃprasthāpya*.
This being the case, in the context of the New Moon sacrifice, the accessory (*guṇa*) called *sākaṃprasthāpya* is prescribed for the sake of the fruit of cattle.
(Regarding the section on the distinctness of sacrifices involving material and deity in the fifth [chapter], Sūtras 12–15:

"And it is a preparatory rite (*saṃskāra*) when there is no specific context (*aprakaraṇa*), because the word does not denote an action. (Jaimini 2.3.12) "Or rather, it is only as much as is stated, because an action has its basis in direct scriptural injunction (*śruti*). (Jaimini 2.3.13)
But the *yajati* (sacrificial act) [is primary] because of the connection of these [words] with the agent who enjoys the fruit of the substance, due to their relationship with the ritual action;
and also because of the observation of indicative marks. (Jaimini Sūtra 2.3.14–15)
He formulates the fifth section:

"A white animal dedicated to Vāyu should be sacrificed for prosperity; likewise, one should offer a *caru* oblation to Sūrya for the sake of great splendor; [this applies] to these two cases of pouring out and measuring with a handful. (MJaiNy 2.3.12)
Or rather, the two qualities [whiteness and being cooked] are prescribed here as qualifiers for the white rice-oblation (caru) or for the ritual action as it has been described,
when performed for the sake of a specific result in a sacrifice.
Whiteness resides in the sacrificial grass touched by the wind, and solar radiance in that which belongs to Agni;
the *caru* is a quality, the *caru* is the vessel, and the pouring out (*nirvāpa*) is dependent upon it.

It is not because of a loss of result; rather, as long as that enjoined action exists, its status as a sacrifice—which necessarily follows from the accomplishment of the form of the substance and so forth—is established by its very purpose. This is taught independently [of any specific ritual context]: "One desiring prosperity should sacrifice a white animal to Vāyu."
And [there is the injunction]: "One desiring spiritual luster (brahmavarcasa) should offer a caru-oblation to Sūrya.
Likewise, this is recited in connection with the New and Full Moon sacrifices: "He should seize the sacrificial animal" and "He offers four handfuls"—this refers to the caru.
The *iṣā* is a long piece of wood like the shaft of a plow, situated on the cart.
Its *ālambha* is the touching of it.
Having referred to this touching of the *iṣā* belonging to the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*), the quality of whiteness is prescribed for that very *iṣā* which is to be touched.
And because that white wood is touched by the wind, its connection with the wind (*vāyavyatā*) is established.
Likewise, having referred to the offering of four handfuls, the *caru* is enjoined as a subordinate quality (*guṇa*).
A *caru* is a cooking vessel (*sthālī*).
And that [offering] is the substratum for the pouring out (nirvāpa).
Because the poured-out oblation belongs to Agni, it is connected with radiance just as the Saura [oblation] is; thus, it is like the Saurya.
Furthermore, regarding the fruits of prosperity and Vedic luster, those belonging to the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices—which fulfill all desires—are merely restated as already established.
Therefore, "it is an injunction of qualities"— this is one prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa).
For it is not appropriate that two words denoting results— which are heard as eternal (nitya), and which serve a purpose— should be either optional restatements (anuvāda) or meaningless (ānarthakya).
Therefore, two distinct rituals qualified by specific qualities and results are enjoined.

Even then, since no sacrifice (*yāga*) is heard of [in the text], and only the touching (*ālambha*) and the pouring out (*nirvāpa*) are heard of, this is an injunction for a ritual exactly as described—this is the second prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*).
[This concerns] the white animal and the *caru* grain-offering.

Since the two deities, Vāyu and Sūrya, are clearly perceived as possessing form, it is impossible to exclude the two sacrifices implied by them; therefore, one must accept the injunction of sacrifices qualified by specific materials and deities. Such an injunction is established by the sense of the texts: "One desiring prosperity should sacrifice with a white animal dedicated to Vāyu" (*vāyavyena śvetena paśunā yajeta*) and "One desiring spiritual luster should sacrifice with a *caru* offering dedicated to Sūrya" (*sauryeṇa caruṇā yajeta*). If it is asked: "What is the status of the two verbal roots—*ālambha* (touching/seizing) and *nirvāpa* (offering)—in the injunction of the necessity to perform the sacrifice, which is itself constituted by the relationship between material and deity, as expressed by the optative suffix (*liṅ*)? [The answer follows:]...
We say it is "reiteration" (anuvāda); this is the established conclusion (siddhānta). MJaiNyC_2,3.12-15 //
(Regarding the sixth section on the sacrificial nature of the touching of the calf and so forth, Sūtras 16–17:
Because it is seen as the predominant meaning in the context;
and because the explanatory passage (arthavāda) is thus rendered consistent. Jaimini 2.3.16–17.
START MJaiNy 2.3.16. The sixth section formulates [the inquiry]:
Is the touching of the six [cups] a sacrifice, or is it a mere touch, like [the touching of] the Vāyavya and other [vessels]? It is a sacrifice.
"Contact [with the calf] would be a purificatory rite (saṃskāra) because of the absence of a deity; it is a purificatory rite based on its position in the sequence of the recitation.

In the section concerning the milking for the Agnihotra, it is heard in scripture: "One should touch the calf. In that regard, the calf to be touched is under dispute: it should be a sacrifice (yajña).
If it is argued that this is because [the sacrifice] has a living being as its substance and object, like the offering to Vāyu, we say no;
for that case is dissimilar due to the absence of a deity.

Furthermore: "This immolation of the calf is a purificatory rite (saṃskāra) that is an auxiliary to the Agnihotra, because it is recited in a section primarily concerned with that [Agnihotra], just like other purificatory rites."
Therefore—the rule concerns the mere contact [of the hand]. (MJaiNyC 2.3.16)
(Sūtra in the section concerning the purpose of the *naivāra-caru* offering in the seventh [book]:
"But that which is connected with a word denoting a purpose is for that purpose, because of its connection with the Vedic text. Jaimini 2.3.18.

The seventh section formulates the problem: "There is a *caru* made of wild rice; he places the *caru*. Is this a sacrifice or a ritual placement (*upadhāna*)? It is a sacrifice, because the deity has been mentioned as a subordinate element. (Mīmāṃsā-jaiminīya-sūtra 2.3.17)
Since there is no certainty regarding a sacrifice, the remainder [of the injunction] need not be considered; therefore, how could there be a root *yaji* (to sacrifice)?
Rather, it remains as merely being placed [as an offering], just as it was stated in the case of the *caru*.
Regarding this, it is heard in the context of the fire-ritual: "The *caru* is made of wild rice (*naivāra*)."
And regarding the statement, "He places the *caru*," a sacrifice having *nīvāra* grain as its sacrificial substance (*dravya*) is enjoined there;
nor is there an absence of a deity (*devatā*) in this case.

Since the deity is established by the supplementary statement, "O Bṛhaspati, this food of yours is indeed the wild rice (nīvāra)," the laying down [of the bricks] is a disposal (*pratipatti*) of that which has been employed in the sacrifice, like the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering and so forth— this being the prima facie view, we reply:
once the injunction for the sacrifice is determined, and the deity is subsequently required, the deity is established by the force of the supplementary statement.
But here, the determination that this is an injunction for a sacrifice is based on the assumption of a deity;
thus, there is mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*).
Therefore, in this case, only the placing (*upadhāna*) is enjoined.

(Aṣṭama Adhikaraṇa: Sūtra on the fact that the *paryagnikaraṇa* is a subordinate quality of the *pātnīvata* offering) "But in the case of the *pātnīvata*, there is a restriction because of its prior occurrence. (Jaimini Sūtra 2.3.19)

The eighth section formulates the problem: "The Pātnīvata, having been carried around with fire, is released"—is this a sacrifice or a subordinate element (guṇa) of a sacrifice? It must be a sacrifice, because of its syntactical connection and lack of intervention. (Mīmāṃsā-Jaiminīya-Nyāyamālā 2.3.19)
Having referred back to the animal that has been recognized [as the same], by means of the word "sacrifice" (utsarga),
the text enjoins the accessory known as "carrying fire around it" (paryagnikaraṇa) for the purpose of precluding subsequent [ritual acts].
In this case, there is no fault in the exclusion [of subsequent acts], because the injunction exists prior to the general rule (codaka);
for the procedure consisting of the subsidiary acts ending with the *paryagnikaraṇa* has its utility already established.

Having introduced the topic with "One should sacrifice an animal dedicated to Tvaṣṭṛ-Patnīvat," the following is prescribed: "They release the Patnīvata animal after it has undergone the *paryagnikaraṇa*."

In this context, since the word *paryagnikṛta* indicates that the animal substance has undergone the consecration (*saṃskāra*), and the word *pātnīvata* indicates its connection with the deity named Patnīvat, this is an injunction for a sacrifice (*yāgavidhi*).

This being the case, the direct syntactical connection (*avyavahitānvaya*) between the words *paryagnikṛta* and *pātnīvata* is obtained. However, according to the final established view (*siddhānta*), they prefer the connection: "They release the animal after it has been *paryagnikṛta*. (*paryagnikṛtam utsṛjanti*).
In that case, a connection with a remote element would be unavoidable.

Therefore, when it is argued that this is an injunction for a sacrifice involving a *paśu* animal dedicated to Soma (*sāyavya*), we reply: because it is taught as an *anārabhyādhīta* (a rule not introduced in the context of a specific ritual), there is no recognition of the subject matter under discussion (*prakṛta*) in the case of the *sāyavya*.
In this case, the animal under discussion, which was introduced as the object to be immolated, is recognized by means of the word *pātnīvata*.

Referring back to that animal, the verbal form "they release" (*utsṛjanti*), conjoined with the term *paryagnikṛta*, enjoins the accessory known as *paryagnikaraṇa* (the rite of carrying fire around).
Nor should it be argued that this injunction is purposeless because the *paryagnikaraṇa* belonging to the archetype is already obtained for the ectype through the rule of transfer (*codaka*).
Because the subsequent members [of the compound] do not follow, and because the *diṭṭhi* (view) serves as the purpose [of the compound].
But if this were the case, it would be a *parisaṃkhyā* (exclusive specification);
and that is corrupted by three defects.
There are three defects: the abandonment of one's own purpose, the acceptance of another's purpose, and the sublation of what has been attained.
In the statement regarding the *paryagnikaraṇa* (circumambulation with fire), its own primary meaning would have to be abandoned,
a prohibition for another purpose would have to be accepted, and the subsequent subsidiary elements obtained through the *codaka* (archetypal injunction) would be sublated.
Not so;

for we do not accept that this is an exclusive specification (*parisaṃkhyā*) stating that "the subsidiary parts (*aṅga*) following the circumambulation with fire (*paryagnikaraṇa*) are not to be performed.
How, then, is their exclusion [established]? We say: it is "implied" (*ārthikī*).

This injunction operates even prior to the application of the *codaka* (the rule of transfer), because a direct instruction (*pratyakṣopadeśa*) generates cognition more swiftly and is therefore stronger than a transfer that must be inferred.

This being the case, since the modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*) has its requirements satisfied by the very auxiliaries directly enjoined, the *codaka* does not apply at all; consequently, the subsequent auxiliaries are not obtained.
Nor should it be said that, by this same reasoning, even those [acts] prior to the *paryagnikaraṇa* would not be obtained;

for since the *paryagnikaraṇa* being enjoined here is something new, there would otherwise be the necessity of postulating a new auxiliary benefit (*upakāra*). Therefore, what is enjoined here is precisely that *paryagnikaraṇa* which, having its benefit already established in the archetype (*prakṛti*), remains in that very state.

Furthermore, since in the archetype (prakṛti) an auxiliary benefit is established as arising from the fire itself immediately after the "prācīnāvīta" rite, here too, because such [a fire] alone is enjoined, the procedure consisting of the subsidiary rites ending with the *paryagnikaraṇa* is established.

This being the case, by the verb "they release" (*utsṛjanti*), the relinquishing of the subsequent subsidiary rites—which is already established when the aforementioned *paryagnikaraṇa* is enjoined—is restated by the verbal root.
Therefore, this is an injunction of a subordinate quality (*guṇavidhi*) in this instance.
(Regarding the ninth [section], the topic concerning whether *adābhya* and others are names of vessels:
Sūtra) Because it is not a substance, it would be a mere subsidiary of the ritual action. Jaimini 2.3.20.
The ninth section formulates the problem:

"Having taken the Adābhya, he takes the Aṃśu"—regarding these two [acts], are they sacrifices or are they subordinate elements (guṇas)? They must be sacrifices because of the names Adābhya and Aṃśu. (Mīmāṃsā Nyāya Prakāśa 2.3.22)
The name [of the sacrifice] would belong to the two *graha* vessels alone because of their immediate sequence;
therefore, the injunction regarding them is a subordinate quality (*guṇa*) for that [sacrifice] by virtue of the sentence that pertains to the Jyotiṣṭoma.
It is heard [in the scripture] without reference to a specific context (*anārabhya*): "He indeed sacrifices with this oblation of curds."
Regarding the statements, "He who, having taken the Adābhya, sacrifices to Soma," and "The life-span and breath indeed depart from him who takes the Aṃśu,"—

in these cases, because the word *adābhya* is the name of a previously unknown rite (apūrva), like *jyotis* and others, a sacrifice bearing that name is enjoined by the verbal suffix in the word *yajate*.
Regarding the term "Aṃśu," although the root *yaj* (to sacrifice) is not explicitly heard here, there is an injunction for a new sacrifice (*apūrvayāga*) solely by virtue of the specific name.
Nor is there an absence of material (*dravya*) and deity (*devatā*) here;

because [the Aṃśu] is a modification (*vikṛti*) of the Jyotiṣṭoma, as indicated by the act of drawing [the cup], its requirements are established through the extension (*atideśa*) of the ritual procedure (*vidhyanta*) of that [archetype] when they are otherwise unobtained—this being the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*).
We reply: Let it be that the words *adābhya* and *aṃśu* are names;
yet those two names would apply only to the two cups (*graha*), not to the two sacrifices (*yāga*).
Because the word "having taken" (*gṛhītvā*) is recited immediately after [the mention of the *aṃśu*], whereas the root *yaji* (to sacrifice) is separated; moreover,
such a root *yaji* does not even exist in the *aṃśu* passage.
Therefore, the injunction here pertains specifically to the two *grahas*.
Furthermore, "taking" (*grahaṇa*) is an accessory (*guṇa*) in the form of a consecration (*saṃskāra*) applied to the Soma juice used in the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice,
because it is identical to the taking of the cups for Indra-Vāyu and others.
Although the Jyotiṣṭoma is not the subject under discussion here, nevertheless, by means of the mention of that which is connected to it, the sentence pertains to the Jyotiṣṭoma.
For this very reason, it is specified as "having taken the Ādābhya cup for Soma."
Alternatively, one should look for the contextually relevant injunctive statement in the sixth chapter, sixth section of the *Taittirīya* [Saṃhitā].
Therefore, it is an injunction of an accessory (*guṇavidhi*) within the *Jyotiṣṭoma*.

(Tenth Section: On the fact that the piling of the fire-altar is a purificatory rite; Sūtras 21–23) "But the word 'Agni' should be understood as denoting a sacrifice, because of the observation of indicative marks. (Jaimini 2.3.21) "Or rather, it should be a substance, because the injunction has that [substance] as its purpose. (Jaimini 2.3.22)
"Due to its connection with that [sacrifice], the ritual act should be named after it; therefore, the injunctions of dharma apply. (Jaimini 2.3.23).
The tenth section formulates [the following]: START MJaiNy 2,3.24-25.
In the passage "One should pile the fire," the root *yaj* (to sacrifice) denotes either the sacrifice itself or a preparatory rite (*saṃskṛti*).

Because of its indicative power (*liṅga*), it is the name of a sacrifice; and since it refers back to the general act of sacrificing (*yajimān*), it is a restatement (*anuvāda*). (Mīmāṃsā Nyāya Mālā 2.3.24)
By conventional usage, this term [citi] is the name of a substance, like the act of placing;
it is a consecration (*saṃskāra*), and once the fire has been consecrated, the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice is prescribed for it.
Having thus enjoined with the words, "He who, knowing thus, piles the fire," it is heard: "Now, therefore, one sacrifices after the fire with the Agniṣṭoma."
"He [attains] him by means of the *ukthya*, him by means of the *ṣoḍaśin*, him by means of the *atirātra*," and so forth.
In this context, the word "Agni" denotes the sacrifice.
Because ritual indicators such as the *stotra* (hymn) and *śastra* (recitation) are heard [in the scriptures],
and that indicator is heard as follows: "The *stotra* of Agni,
the *śastra* of Agni."
And [it is said]: "There are six *upasads* for one who has recourse to the fire.

If the indicative mark (*liṅga*) depends on that which provides the application, then let the restatement (*anuvāda*) by means of the root *yaj* (to sacrifice) occur in that which provides the application.

In the sentence "He performs the sacrifice for Agni with the Agniṣṭoma," because of the grammatical coordination (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) between "Agni" and "yajati" (he sacrifices), this is the name of a sacrifice, just as in the case of "He sacrifices silently" (*upāṃśu yajati*). Now, if it were argued that because the word *anu* is construed with the word *agni*, the *agniṣṭoma* is what is to be sacrificed to subsequently— nevertheless, only when there has been a prior sacrifice to Agni can a subsequent sacrifice (*anuyajana*) to the *agniṣṭoma* be possible.
In the case of "Yajñadatta follows Devadatta," [the latter's action is understood] because Devadatta is seen to be moving in front.

Therefore, in the statement "He piles the fire-altar" (*agniṃ cinute*), a sacrifice named "Agni" is enjoined by the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*). As for the root *cinoti* (to pile), it is a restatement (*anuvāda*) of the piling (*cayana*) already established by the sentence "He piles the fire-altar with bricks," just as the collection of cups (*grahasamudāya*) is established as a modification (*vikṛti*) of the Soma sacrifice. This being the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), [we reply]:
We reply: the word *agni* denotes the substance fire by conventional usage (*rūḍhi*).

And since conventional usage, being already established, is stronger than the denotation of a sacrifice which must be inferred from indicators (*liṅga*) and other means, it does not function as the name of a sacrifice.
And there is no similarity here [to the case of the fire-drill],
because both the substance and the cause are unestablished.

Therefore, since the act of "laying" (ādhāna) has been enjoined by the statement "one should lay the fire," the "piling" (cayana) enjoined by the statement "one piles the fire" is a refinement (*saṃskāra*) of the substance that is the fire.
Nor is there an absence of application for the consecrated object,

because its application in the Agniṣṭoma and other rites is established by such sentences as "One sacrifices with the Agniṣṭoma [using] fire. Therefore, it is an injunction of consecration (saṃskāravidhi).
(Regarding the eleventh section, concerning the status of the *māsāgnihotra* and other rites as distinct sacrifices, the sūtra states:
"In a different context, there is a difference in purpose. (Jaimini Sūtra 2.3.24)
He formulates the eleventh topic: "One offers the Agnihotra for a month"—is this an accessory (guṇa) or a different rite?
Having referred back to the established rite, the unestablished month is here enjoined as an accessory. (MJaiNy 2.3.26)

"Having performed the Upasad rites"—this [phrase] refers to the obligatory [rites], because those [specific rites] are impossible [in this context], and because there is no injunction for multiple [acts]; therefore, it is another action due to the difference in context (prakaraṇāntara).
In the Kuṇḍapāyinām Ayana, it is heard: "Having performed the Upasad rites, one offers the Agnihotra for a month; one should sacrifice with the Darśapūrṇamāsa for a month."
If it is argued here that, having referred to the already established *nitya-agnihotra*, a new quality characterized by the month (*māsa*) is enjoined because it was not previously obtained—
this is not so.
Is it the month itself that is being enjoined?
Regarding the phrase "having performed the *upasad*s," even as for those *upasad*s mentioned there:
the first [alternative] is not tenable,
because in your own view, even the *upasad*s— being devoid of the attainment of the obligatory *agnihotra*— must themselves be enjoined.

Not the second [alternative], because if it were an injunction of multiple qualities regarding an action already established, it would result in the fallacy of sentence-splitting (*vākya-bheda*). [Objection:
Well then, let it not be an injunction of qualities.
If it is asked, "What is the proof that this is a different ritual action?
we reply: "It is a different context" (*prakaraṇāntara*).
This is not the context of the obligatory Agnihotra.
Because it is not proximate;
for this is the section concerning the *ayana*,
as it has been taught starting from the *ayana*.
If it is asked, "What then is the basis for the suspicion that this is an injunction of a subordinate quality (*guṇavidhi*) regarding the obligatory *agnihotra*?"—[the answer is:
even though the context (*prakaraṇa*) does not provide such a connection, this suspicion arises because the term *agnihotra* itself provides it;
and that suspicion is refuted by the consequence of splitting the sentence (*vākyabheda*).

This being the case, once the power of the word *agnihotra*— which was intended to establish a subordinate element by setting aside the self-evident difference of context and effecting a unity of context— is obstructed, that very difference of context remains and distinguishes this ritual from the obligatory *agnihotra*.
It will be stated in the seventh book that the two words *agnihotra* serve for the purpose of extending the properties (*dharma*) [of the original rite].
If it is argued: "Surely this rite is enjoined as qualified by the month and the Upasads;
therefore, due to the difference in accessories (guṇa), there is a difference in the rites according to the Vājina-nyāya, not due to a difference in context (prakaraṇa)," we say: no.
Because of the disparity:
"The quality [of speed] is to be enjoined as something to be adopted,
whereas the month is not so"— this is another disparity.

In ultimate reality, however, it is the difference of context (prakaraṇabheda), which is perceived even earlier here, that establishes the difference of action, and the difference of quality merely reinforces it.
Therefore, in this case, the difference of context alone is the cause of the distinction.
(Regarding the twelfth [section], the section on optional sacrifices to Agni and others, there is the sūtra:
"And the fruit [is enjoined] when not in proximity to an action. Jaimini 2.3.25.

He formulates the twelfth section: "The eight-pot-sherd offering for Agni is for one desiring luster; is this the fruit of the archetypal rite, or is it the fruit of another action? Because [the fruit] is mentioned [directly], the previous principle does not apply. (Mīmāṃsā-jaiminīya-sūtra 2.3.28)

Let it not be that the context is split [and thus constitutes] a separate ritual action, because of the lack of proximity; for this form, taught as an independent injunction (*anārabhyādhīta*), is observed to be complete in all its parts. Regarding this, it is heard in an independent injunction: "One desiring splendor should offer a cake on eight potsherds to Agni."
"One desiring splendor [should sacrifice] on a tree.

Here, having referred to the Āgneya sacrifice which constitutes the archetype (*prakṛti*) of the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*), the fruit consisting of the desire for splendor is prescribed therein.
Why?

Because the connection between the Agneya sacrifice and its fruit is established by the sentence itself; nor can it be a separate rite according to the previously mentioned principle of the "month-long Agnihotra," because of the disparity between the two cases.
In that case, because it was taught in connection with a specific context (*ārambha*), there is indeed a difference of context (*prakaraṇāntaratva*).
Here, however, since it is taught as not being connected to a specific context (*anārabhyādhītatva*), there is no context at all;
how then could there be a difference of context here?
Furthermore, the month is not something to be undertaken as a primary objective,
because it is impossible to accomplish it merely by following the Agnihotra; however, the fruit is indeed to be undertaken.

Since it is possible to desire splendor by following the *Āgneya* [offering] of the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*), the position reached is that this is an injunction of a result (*phalavidhi*).

To this, we reply: even though there is no difference in context (*prakaraṇāntara*), because it is taught as an independent injunction (*anārabhyādhīta*), there is indeed a lack of proximity (*asaṃnidhi*).
It is that very [act] which differentiates the ritual action here;

nor is there a differentiation of the ritual action according to the logic of the *vājina* offering, because the form consisting of the eight-potherd substance and the deity Agni is identical in both cases.

If it is argued that even the state of being a different context (*prakaraṇāntaratva*) is caused by non-proximity (*asaṃnidhi*), and thus non-proximity alone is the cause for the distinction between ritual acts— as in the case of the *māsāgnihotra*— then let this [distinction] be merely an elaboration of that very [non-proximity].
Furthermore, the result (*phala*) is non-adoptable (*anupādeya*), just like the month.
Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence that [the action] would be fruitless, like a mere means of proof (*sādhana*).
Furthermore, desire arises spontaneously from the knowledge of the beauty of the object;
it does not come into being through the hearing of an injunction (*vidhi*).
Whether there is a difference in the logical principle (*nyāya*) regarding the two loci, or whether there is a unity of the logical principle,
in any case, the *tejaskāmeṣṭi* is a distinct ritual action (*karmāntara*).

This same principle is to be observed in those passages recited in the section on optional sacrifices (*kāmyeṣṭi*), such as "One desiring offspring should offer a cake on eleven potsherds to Indra and Agni," and so forth. (MJaiNyC 2.3.28–29)
(Thirteenth [Topic]: The Section on the *Aveṣṭi* Having Food as its Fruit;
Sūtra) "But because there is no distinction in proximity, the restatement is for the sake of the fruit. (Jaimini 2.3.26)

The thirteenth section formulates the following: "In the case of 'one should sacrifice on the full moon,' 'as long as one lives,' and likewise 'desiring food, etc., by this [rite],' is there a difference of ritual acts or is it a subordinate element (guṇa)? (Mīmāṃsā-jaiminīya-sūtra 2.3.30).

Because the injunction and the material are one, and because place and so forth do not arise [from them], when an injunction of the action is necessary, their distinction [is established] through repetition. (MJaiNy 2.3.31)
Since the connection with place and so forth has not [otherwise] been obtained, there is no injunction; for there is no identity between the two.
Because of the activity of the word "man" (puṃśabda), it is restated as a reiteration (anuvāda).

In the context of the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, place, time, and occasion are prescribed: "One should sacrifice on level ground," "One should sacrifice on the full moon day," and "One should sacrifice with the Darśapūrṇamāsa throughout one's life."

In the context of the Aveṣṭi sacrifice, the result is recorded: "One should cause him who desires food to sacrifice with this [offering]. By the word "etcetera" (ādi), the consecration (saṃskāra) is included;
and that is recorded in the context of the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices: "He cuts off the remnant for the Sviṣṭakṛt."
In that regard, place, time, cause, fruit, and purificatory rites (saṃskāra) are not to be adopted because they are not to be performed;
for this very reason, they are not things to be enjoined (vidheya),
since "adoption" (upādāna) and "injunction" (vidhi) are synonymous.
Therefore, one must necessarily accept that this is a rule regarding ritual action (*karmavidhi*).

In this regard, since the Darśa and other sacrifices previously enjoined as the subject of the context (*prakaraṇin*) are being enjoined again by these sentences, the opponent argues that—just as in the case of "he offers the Samidhs" (*samidho yajati*) and so forth—a distinction of actions arises from mere repetition (*abhyāsa*).
To this we reply: even though location and the like are not themselves things to be enjoined, let their connection with the enjoined action be what is enjoined.
Furthermore, since that [injunction] was not previously prescribed like the action itself, it has not been established and thus requires an injunction.
As for what was said— that "the terms 'appropriation' (upādāna) and 'injunction' (vidhi) are synonyms"— that is incorrect.

Injunction (*vidhi*) is the instigation of what has not yet begun; it is the operation of the word directed toward a person. Appropriation (*upādāna*) is the performance of that which has not yet been performed.
Furthermore, there is a great difference [between these cases]: that action is not the object [of the injunction], whereas the human effort (puruṣavyāpāra) is.

As for the re-injunction of the *darśa* and other sacrifices, that too is a restatement (*anuvāda*) of the action for the purpose of enjoining its connection with place and so forth; thus, it does not bring about a difference in the action.

In cases such as "He offers the *samidh*s," since there is no other quality to be enjoined and a restatement is therefore impossible, the re-enjoinment causes a difference in the action—this is the distinction. // MJaiNyC_2,3.30-32 //

(Section 14: On the fact that the double mention of the *Āgneya* hymn is for the purpose of praise; Sūtras 27–29) Because it is the cause of the *Āgneya* hymn, it should be understood through repetition. (Jaimini 2.3.27) But because there is no division of the rites, it is not enjoined by the double mention. (Jaimini 2.3.28)
Or rather, the restatement is for another purpose. (Jaimini Sūtra 2.3.29).
He formulates the fourteenth section as follows:
The Āgneya sacrifice mentioned in the context of the Darśapūrṇamāsa may be performed independently as well;
however, the statements "yad darśe" and so forth refer either to a different ritual or are merely explanatory restatements (anuvāda).
Due to repetition, there is a difference in action; let it be performed twice in the Darśeṣṭi sacrifice.
Because of the recognition of oneness, the praise of the Aindrāgna offering is made by means of the anuvāka.
"That which belongs to Agni, the cake on eight potsherds, is never omitted on the new moon day and the full moon day."
Thus, [the offering] is enjoined at two times;

however, "The cake on eight potsherds for Agni is offered on the new moon day" enjoin it again at one time. In that case, there is a distinction [of the act] due to repetition characterized by an unqualified re-enunciation, just as in the case of the *prayāja* offerings.
If it is argued that, such being the case, there would be a double performance of the Āgneya sacrifice at the time of the New Moon (darśa), we say no;
for since the Āgneya is a single entity due to recognition, the statement regarding the same time is merely a restatement (anuvāda).
Nor is a restatement purposeless.
This is because it serves the purpose of praising Indra and Agni as the deities to be enjoined.
Even though the cake on eight potsherds dedicated to Agni (āgneya) is offered on the new moon day,
nevertheless, it does not become effective through Agni alone.
Agni accompanied by Indra is more effective;
therefore,
the statement "the offering to Indra and Agni must be performed" is a praise of the injunction.
However, the discrepancy regarding the *prayāja* offerings has already been stated and should be kept in mind.
Thus ends the third quarter of the second chapter in the *Jaiminīyanyāyamālāvistara* by the illustrious Mādhava.
(Now begins the fourth quarter of the second chapter) (In the first section concerning the lifelong Agnihotra, Sūtras 1–7).
The lifelong practice is a property of the ritual action, because of the context (Jaimini 2.4.1);
or rather, it belongs to the performer, because of its connection with the scriptural injunction (Jaimini 2.4.2).

Furthermore, because of the observation of indicative marks; for if it were a property of the ritual action, it would be restricted by the commencement [of the rite], and in that case, the other [lifelong] requirement would be rendered purposeless (Jaimini 2.4.3).

And [the scripture] shows [the completion of the sacrifice] at the time of the conclusion; if there were a difference in the ritual acts based on time, [it would be so], but because of impermanence, it cannot be thus. Furthermore, there is a contradiction as before.
But because of the restriction on the agent, the scriptural injunction regarding time should be a contingent occasion (*nimitta*).
[Jaimini Sūtra 2.4.7] The first section of the fourth quarter formulates the argument as follows:
"One offers for as long as one lives" (yāvajjīvaṃ juhoti) is a rule (dharma) regarding the action or the agent;
because it is a matter of time, it is a property of the action. Therefore, let the optional rite (kāmya) alone be performed.
Time is not the life-force itself, because of the distinction between the causal factors;

thus, the performance for a specific desire would be distinct from the lifelong performance. (Mīmāṃsā-sūtra 2.4.2) — In the Bahvṛca Brāhmaṇa it is heard: "One performs the Agnihotra as long as one lives."
In this context, the word "as long as life" (*yāvajjīva*) refers to a period of time delimited by death.

Furthermore, since a connection with that period of time was not previously established for the *kāmya-agnihotra* under discussion, it is enjoined in relation to the act already referred to by the word "he offers" (*juhoti*).

This being the case, because this sentence lacks the status of an injunction for a compulsory (*nitya*) performance, the single optional (*kāmya*) performance of the Agnihotra enjoined by another sentence remains the only one applicable.
And that optional performance must be practiced repeatedly;

for a single performance is already established by the injunction "one desiring heaven should offer the Agnihotra," and because the injunction regarding time, "as long as one lives," would otherwise be rendered meaningless.
Therefore, this is an injunction regarding the nature of time for the sake of accomplishing the practice of optional (kāmya) karma.
This being the position reached, we reply:
the word "yāvajjīvam" (as long as one lives) is not a denoter of time.
However, it is indicative (lakṣaka);
the literal meaning (vācyārtha), on the other hand, is "the entirety of life.
And life cannot be enjoined as a duty pertaining to ritual action (karma).
Because that [quality] is a characteristic of the person;
and having made that characteristic of the person the basis for the sign (*nimitta*), the performance of the *agnihotra* is enjoined.
Furthermore, there is no division of the ritual action (*karmabheda*) here.
This is because other words and such factors, which would serve as its causes, are absent;
nor is repetition its cause,
since there is no absence of repetition due to the presence of a specific motive.
Therefore, a distinction in the application [of the rite] results,
because living is the occasion here;
since it is impossible to abandon that which is occasioned when the occasion exists, its obligatory nature is established by implication.
Nor does it follow that there must be a continuity of performance due to the continuity of the cause for living,
because [the rites] are prescribed for the evening and morning times. Therefore, since living is a property of the person, the obligatory (*nitya*) and optional (*kāmya*) performances are distinct.
(Section on the Unity of Ritual Action Based on All Branches, Sūtras 8–32):

"On account of differences in name, form, and ritual details, repetition, censure, incapacity, statements of completion, expiation, and the observation of other purposes, there would be a difference in the ritual action across different branches" (Jaimini 2.4.8). "Or rather, it is one [action], because there is no difference in connection, form, injunction, and name" (Jaimini 2.4.9).
It cannot be [determined] by name, because it is not a designation based on an injunction (Jaimini 2.4.10).
Furthermore, all [the acts] would constitute a single ritual action (Jaimini 2.4.11).
And the name is something artificially created (Jaimini 2.4.12).

Even if [the knowledge] is one, the rule of conduct applies to the Vidyā; (Jaimini 2.4.13). The scriptural injunction regarding the Vidyā is like that of the Āgneya sacrifice; (Jaimini 2.4.14). It is a restatement, as in the case of the Āgneya; (Jaimini 2.4.15).
Or rather, there is no repetition because there is no distinction in the connection with the Vedic text (Jaimini 2.4.16);
and because of the non-proximity of the purpose (Jaimini 2.4.17);
nor is it enjoined for only one (Jaimini 2.4.18).
And because of the mention of completion, there is the expectation [of a single performance].

(Jaimini 2.4.19) Even though there is unity [of the rite], there are subsequent statements regarding censure, incapacity, and completion. (Jaimini 2.4.20) Expiation occurs on account of a specific occasion. (Jaimini 2.4.21)
Or rather, by necessity due to the context;

the completion [of the sacrifice] is understood as before, just as it is known. (Jaimini 2.4.22) The indicative mark (*liṅga*) is not restricted, because it is subsidiary to all [the days]; for there is no injunction of a ritual action (*karmacodanā*) therein. Therefore, the designation "day" (*ahāra*) should apply to the twelve-day rite (*dvādaśāha*). (Jaimini 2.4.23–24)

And because the substances are not enjoined, there would be a lack of fixed determination for the injunctions; [however], it would be fixed due to the specific direction, therefore it must be a permanent restatement (*nityānuvāda*).

(Jaimini 2.4.25) Because of the prohibition of what has been enjoined, there would be an excess in one alternative case. (Jaimini 2.4.26) In the case of the Sārasvata sacrifice, because of the conflict, it should be "when" (*yadā*) [the moon rises]. (Jaimini 2.4.27)
In the Upahavya sacrifice, there is no counter-exception;
rather, the repetition of the scriptural statement is for the sake of a specific quality,
and it also demonstrates the authoritative cognition [of that quality].
Alternatively, due to the connection with the sequence, the distinctness of the injunctions would be restricted to a single [action].

(Jaimini Sūtra 2.4.31) But because there is no connection with anything contradictory, there is unity of action; since they are connected [with that], there would be the cognition of all actions as being enjoined.
(Jaimini Sūtra 2.4.32)
The second section formulates the inquiry:
Is there a difference of ritual action due to the difference of Vedic recensions, or not?
Here, the ritual action is indeed differentiated.
The names such as "Kāṭhaka" and so forth are observed to be causes for many divisions [of the Veda].
"For these causes of distinction are joined [to the action] by means of the book and so forth;
however, because of the recognition of the form and other attributes, the action is understood to be non-different.
(Mīmāṃsā-sūtra 2.4.4) The ritual known as the Darśapūrṇamāsa is taught in various recensions (śākhās), such as the Kāṭhaka, Kāṇva, Mādhyaṃdina, and Taittirīya.
In that regard, the ritual action differs according to the difference in Vedic branches.
Why?
Because many causes of differentiation, such as differences in name and so forth, are observed.
The distinction of names such as the Kāṭhaka and the Kāṇva [is based on this].
Certain followers of a Vedic branch who study the *kārīrī* passages practice eating on the ground, whereas those studying other branches do not so practice.
Thus is the differentiation of dharma:
the mantras such as "For food, thee" (iṣe tvā) and so forth, as well as the ritual acts such as the cutting of the palāśa branch, which have been studied in one particular recensional branch (śākhā).
The statement "they are studied even in other recensions" is a repetition [of this point].
In this way, incapacity and other such factors may be cited as reasons for the division [of the Veda].
For indeed, it is not possible for a short-lived human being to perform ritual actions preceded by the study of all recensions.
Therefore, since there is a difference of ritual action due to the difference of Vedic recensions— this being the position reached—
we reply: the ritual action is one, because there is no difference in its form and other characteristics.
The form of the sacrifice, such as the *āgneya-aṣṭākapāla* and others, which exists in one recensional branch (*śākhā*),
is found in other branches as well; likewise,
the human activity consisting of the sacrifice, expressed as "one should sacrifice with the New and Full Moon sacrifices" (*darśapūrṇamāsābhyāṃ yajeta*), is of a single kind.
The name of the rite, "the New and Full Moon sacrifices" (*darśapūrṇamāsau*), is one;
the connection with the result, "one who desires heaven" (*svargakāmaḥ*), is also one. Therefore, the rite is a single, undivided act.
The arguments for the prima facie position (pūrvapakṣa), however, are consistent otherwise:
the *Kāṭhaka* and other such texts are not ritual manuals (*karmasāman*), unlike the *Jyotiḥ* and others, because there is no scriptural injunction such as "one should sacrifice with the *Kāṭhaka*."
From the usage "he studies the Kāṭhaka," it should be understood that [the term refers to] a book;
the duties of study, such as [rules regarding] the ground and food, apply [to the student];
and repetition is not faulty because of the difference between the students.
Even one of short life may be able to perform the ritual by means of the principle of synthesis (*upasaṃhāra*) found in other recensional branches (*śākhā*).

Therefore: "Because of recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*) of the form [of the rite] as not being established otherwise, the ritual action does not differ even when there is a difference in recensional branches. (MJaiNyC 2.4.3–4)
Thus ends the fourth quarter of the second chapter in the *Jaiminīyanyāyamālāvistara* composed by the venerable Mādhava;
the second chapter is completed.
